docs.title: GemPBA
docs.text:
GemPBA (Generic Massive Parallelisation of Branching Algorithms) parallelizes branch-and-bound, backtracking and other recursive search algorithms. Its core is C++23, for speed, and it is just as much a Java library: the same runtime is on Maven Central as io.github.rapastranac:gempba, and a C ABI opens it to other languages. It runs a search on:

  • Multithreading: all the cores of one machine, with nothing else to install
  • MPI: many processes across many nodes, over the Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI you already have
  • Hybrid: several threads per process, spread across nodes

  • C++

    find_package(gempba), plus COMPONENTS mpi for MPI, from APT, Homebrew or MSYS2.

    Install for C++ · Quick Start

  • Java

    io.github.rapastranac:gempba or gempba-mpi on Maven Central, no token, natives inside the JAR.

    Install for Java · Quick Start

docs.title: What's new in v5
docs.text:
• One core, one entry point

    No more build-time flavors: one library with multithreading built in, and MPI as a component you ask for. Every rank calls scheduler::run, with the same API in C++ and Java.

    Architecture

  • MPI your way

    The MPI component compiles in your build against the MPI you have: Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI. Switching MPIs is a new build directory, not a reinstall.

    Installation

  • Exact termination

    A run ends exactly when its work is done: Dijkstra–Scholten acknowledgements, with no timeout and no heuristic. v5 drops the old timeout parameter for good.

    How the run ends

  • Stop a run, know how it ended

    Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, request_stop() or a dashboard wind a run down gracefully, keeping its best result, and every run says whether that result is proven.

    Stopping a Run

  • Java on Maven Central

    One dependency, no repository or token, with Linux, Windows and Apple Silicon natives inside the JAR, and your own native when you need another MPI.

    Java

  • In MSYS2's own repository

    On Windows, pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba installs GemPBA from MSYS2's UCRT64 repository, next to apt on Ubuntu and brew on macOS.

    Installation

  • A clean shared library

    libgempba.so.5 exports only its API, keeps its dependencies private, and its headers include only the standard library.

    Releases

docs.title: The research behind it
docs.text:
Two research contributions are baked into the framework.

The first is the Quasi-Horizontal Load Balancing strategy. Standard work-stealing treats all pending tasks equally. Quasi-horizontal balancing understands the shape of your recursion tree and selects work near the root, where each task will spawn the most downstream work. For branching algorithms where subtree sizes vary dramatically, this makes a significant difference in CPU utilization.

The second is the Semi-Centralized Scheduler. Distributing work across processes sounds straightforward until you hit the rejected task problem: a worker receives a task, but by the time it arrives the worker is already busy and has to bounce it back to the sender. Do this naively and you spend more time rerouting work than doing it. The semi-centralized design avoids this by keeping a lightweight coordinator that never holds tasks itself but maintains global priority awareness. The coordinator always knows which worker is idle and routes tasks directly there, eliminating the bounce-back problem without becoming a bottleneck.

For the full performance analysis and formal description, see:

  • MSc. Thesis
  • Paper in Parallel Computing

Explore the internals

For a navigable, AI-assisted deep-dive into GemPBA's architecture and source, browse the GemPBA DeepWiki — auto-generated and refreshed periodically.

docs.title: GemPBA Dashboard
docs.text:
A desktop app that connects to a running GemPBA program and shows the whole run live: every node and rank, the cores working, the tasks moving between them, idle time and memory as they change.

  • See the whole run at a glance: a summary on top, one live tile per node below.
  • Drill into any node, socket or rank for its CPU, tasks, idle time, memory and busiest peers.
  • Connect locally, to a host over SSH, or straight to an HPC compute node through an MFA login node, with no manual tunnel.

See the dashboard Download

docs.title: The core and the MPI component
docs.text:
GemPBA is one library with multithreading built in, plus an optional MPI component, on any platform:

  • The core (gempba) — uses all cores of a single machine; no MPI needed.
  • The MPI component (gempba-mpi) — distributes work across multiple machines/nodes over MPI. It installs as source, and your build compiles it against your MPI.

A program uses the MPI component only when it asks for it, so multithreading and MPI programs build side by side from one installation. See Installation for APT / MSYS2 / Homebrew instructions and find_package(gempba COMPONENTS mpi), and Architecture for how the pieces fit.

Using Java?

The Java API is the same core from the JVM, as gempba and gempba-mpi on Maven Central. See the Java section.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: GemPBA is a high-performance C++ core with a Java API and a C ABI on top. Since v3.0 it has followed one guiding principle: the public API should be simple and template-free, while everything underneath should be pluggable. v5.0.0 takes that to the packaging and the entry point: one library, one way to start a run, and MPI only when you ask for it.

docs.title: One core, plus a component
docs.text:
v4 against v5: v4 built two flavors and a program picked one at build time; v5 is one core library with multithreading built in, plus an MPI component a program asks for v4: two flavors, chosen at build time v5: one core, plus a component libgempba multithreading gempba::multithreading COMPONENTS mt libgempba-mpi one MPI per package gempba::multiprocessing GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING A program picks one flavor; mt and mpi can't be used together Java: io.gempba:gempba, mt / mp-mpi classifiers, from GitHub Packages with a token Your program, multithreading or MPI libgempba.so.5 gempba::gempba nodes · node manager load balancers · thread pool scheduler interface telemetry · C ABI gempba::mpi on request MPI schedulers MPI telemetry built against your MPI always if asked Java: io.github.rapastranac:gempba and gempba-mpi, on Maven Central, no token

Up to v4, you chose a flavor when you built gempba: multithreading or MPI, each with its own namespace (gempba::multithreading, gempba::multiprocessing) and its own library, and one program could never use both. v5 replaces the flavors with one core, gempba::gempba, which has multithreading built in: the nodes, the node manager, the load balancers, the thread pool, the scheduler interface, telemetry and the C ABI. The MPI component, gempba::mpi, adds the schedulers that spread a run across MPI ranks, and a program asks for it with find_package(gempba COMPONENTS mpi). Multithreading and MPI programs build side by side from one installation, and the calls read the same in both: an MPI program creates its scheduler with gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(...) and passes it to gempba::create_load_balancer(...) and gempba::create_node_manager(...), and a multithreading program passes none.

The core is a shared library, libgempba.so.5 on Linux and libgempba.dll on Windows. It exports only its public API: spdlog and fmt are compiled into it, hwloc is a private dependency it loads at run time, and its public headers include only the C++ standard library. Your build looks for nothing else.

docs.title: MPI, built against yours
docs.text:
The MPI component is compiled against your MPI: the installation holds the core library and the component's source; find_package(gempba COMPONENTS mpi) compiles gempba::mpi in your build against the MPI CMake finds there, Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI, and your program links both Installed once Your build Your program libgempba.so.5 compiled, shared + headers gempba-mpi the component, as source compiled in your build find_package(gempba COMPONENTS mpi) compiles gempba::mpi, static, against the MPI it finds Open MPI MPICH MS-MPI whichever MPI your build sees links gempba::gempba gempba::mpi your MPI Another MPI: another build directory, not a reinstall

The MPI component installs as source. find_package(gempba COMPONENTS mpi) compiles it in your build into a static gempba::mpi, against the MPI CMake finds there: Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI. Before v5, each package's MPI part was compiled against one MPI and worked only with it. Two things follow:

  • Your compiler must be compatible with the one that built libgempba.
  • Switching MPIs takes another build directory, not a reinstall.

The Java artifacts can't compile anything on your machine, so gempba-mpi's bundled native targets one MPI per OS, Open MPI on Linux and macOS and MS-MPI on Windows, and -Dgempba.native.path loads one you built against another (see Which MPI).

docs.title: One entry point on every rank
Exact termination
docs.text: An MPI run ends exactly when its work is done, with no timeout and no quiet period to wait out. Since v4.3.0, both schedulers detect termination with Dijkstra–Scholten acknowledgements: every task sent is acknowledged, a rank acknowledges the task that woke it only once its own work and everything it sent are finished, and rank 0, which never waits on anyone, knows the search is over when its last acknowledgement arrives. So a run can't end early with a task in flight, or late because a message was slow. How the run ends walks through it, and v5.0.0 removed the old timeout parameter from create_scheduler.

docs.title: How a run ends
docs.text:
How a run ends: completed, with a proven result; interrupted by a signal, the stop call or the dashboard, with the best result found before the stop; or lost, killed without warning, with no outcome, no log line and no final telemetry line Completed The whole search space was explored result proven run_outcome COMPLETED log info: run completed final line {"reason":"completed"} Interrupted Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, request_stop(), or the dashboard result best found before the stop run_outcome INTERRUPTED + trigger log warning, naming the trigger final line "interrupted" + "trigger" Lost SIGKILL, a crash, a node failure result none returned run_outcome none log no end line final line none: the stream just closes

A run can also be stopped early, from code, by a signal or from a dashboard, and it says which of the three ways it ended. Stopping a Run covers each trigger in C++ and Java.

docs.title: Pluggable underneath
docs.text:
Every major component is defined by an interface: the load balancer, the scheduler, the node implementation. You can replace any of them without touching user code. The default implementations cover the common cases; if you have specialized hardware or a domain-specific scheduling strategy, you implement the interface and plug it in. A custom scheduler runs on MPI, the one backend gempba ships.

What this means in practice: a multithreading program includes one header, <gempba/gempba.hpp>, and an MPI program adds <gempba/mpi.hpp>. You call a handful of factory functions and wrap your recursive branches in nodes, naming your function's types when you create one. The template machinery (function signature matching, IPC serialization, thread pool management) lives in detail/ and stays there. The load balancer does not know your function signatures. The scheduler does not know your argument types. Everything is decoupled through interfaces, which is exactly why it can be this clean from the outside.

docs.title: Telemetry, the C ABI and Java
docs.text:
The runtime carries a built-in telemetry subsystem beneath the public API, which the GemPBA Dashboard reads live. The whole runtime is also exposed through a C ABI, <gempba/cabi/gempba.h> plus <gempba/cabi/gempba_mpi.h> for the MPI component, and the Java API sits on it: the same core, from the JVM, on Maven Central.

The API Reference section documents each public header and what it does.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
GemPBA started as a research project during my MSc at Université de Sherbrooke, under the supervision of Professor Manuel Lafond. His work sits at the intersection of algorithm theory and bioinformatics: reconstructing evolutionary histories, solving gene reconciliation problems, and tackling NP-hard combinatorial questions that arise naturally when comparing genomes across species. Problems like weighted quartet consensus, phylogenetic network recognition, and maximum common contractions are all computationally hard, and branch-and-bound is one of the few practical approaches for finding exact solutions to them at meaningful scale.

My own focus was high-performance computing. Combining that with bioinformatics was not an obvious match at first glance, but it turned out that evolutionary biology is remarkably good at producing problems that no computer wants to solve. That made it a great fit. GemPBA is what came out of that overlap.

docs.title: What it is built for
docs.text:
Any algorithm that explores a search tree by branching on decisions and pruning dead ends can benefit from GemPBA. The framework handles the parallel infrastructure so you can focus on the algorithm itself.

Concrete problem domains where this applies:

  • Bioinformatics — phylogenetic tree reconstruction, gene tree reconciliation, orthology prediction, and other combinatorial problems in comparative genomics
  • Graph problems — maximum clique, minimum vertex cover, graph coloring, subgraph isomorphism
  • Routing and scheduling — vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, traveling salesman variants
  • Constraint satisfaction — exact solvers for assignment and packing problems
  • Operations research — integer programming subproblems solved via branch-and-bound

The common thread is a search space that is too large to enumerate naively but structured enough that pruning eliminates most of it. GemPBA distributes that search across threads and processes, with load balancing strategies designed for the unbalanced trees these problems produce in practice.

docs.title: The research
docs.text: The framework was published in Parallel Computing (2023) and the full design is described in my MSc thesis. The two main contributions, quasi-horizontal load balancing and the semi-centralized scheduler, are described in the Why GemPBA page.

docs.title: Reporting bugs and proposing features
docs.text: Open a GitHub Issue on the main repository. Search existing issues before submitting to avoid duplicates. A good report includes a clear summary of the problem, what behavior you expected and what you actually observed, and a minimal reproducible example where possible.

docs.title: Submitting changes
docs.text: Pull the latest main before creating a branch. Fork the repository, create a branch, make your changes, and open a pull request against main.

docs.title: Branch naming
docs.text:
Every branch must be tied to an issue. The branch name is derived directly from the issue title, converted to kebab-case and prefixed with the issue number:

{issue-number}-{issue-title-in-kebab-case}

For example, an issue numbered 8 titled "Reformat interface reference pages" becomes:

8-reformat-interface-reference-pages

If multiple iterations of work are needed on the same issue, append a double dash followed by a short description of what that iteration specifically addresses:

8-reformat-interface-reference-pages--fix-anchors

Create the issue first if one does not exist, then open the branch with its number as the prefix.

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
Keep commits atomic — one logical unit per commit, never bundling unrelated changes. Every commit must leave the project in a working state. Start the title with the issue number and one type: feat, fix, perf, refactor, docs, test, build, ci or chore. When the commit changes work an earlier, already merged issue brought, name that issue in parentheses:

#8 docs: Reformat node_traits reference to table-driven style
#465 feat(#45, #394): Log how the run ended

For multi-change commits, add a blank line after the title and describe each change as a bullet:

#8 docs: Reformat node_traits reference to table-driven style

- Replace prose description with a two-column table
- Add anchor for each trait entry

Skip the body entirely for single-change commits.

If a bug is introduced in the current unmerged branch, fold the fix back into the commit that introduced it — do not add a follow-up "fix" commit.

Add tests for new functionality and update the documentation where relevant.

docs.title: Pull request
docs.text:
Open the PR against main. The PR title must match the issue title verbatim. If the branch covers a specific iteration, append an em-dash and a short iteration summary:

Reformat interface reference pages — fix anchors

CI runs automatically on every push to the branch and when the PR is opened; all checks must pass before merging. The default merge strategy is a merge commit — do not squash or rebase.

Use the following structure for the PR description (omit Tests if there are none):

**Problem**
- What was broken or missing.

**Fix / Solution**
- What was changed and why (at the decision level, not line-by-line).

**Tests**
- What was tested and how.

docs.title: Coding style
docs.text:
Avoid code comments by default. A comment is only justified when the why cannot be inferred from the code itself: a hidden constraint, a platform quirk, a non-obvious invariant, or a deliberate workaround. Never narrate what the code does — well-named identifiers already do that. Rationale for workarounds or platform-specific decisions belongs in the commit body or PR description.

Code style is also enforced by clang-format and clang-tidy, both configured at the repository root.

docs.title: Formatting (.clang-format)
docs.text:
Based on the LLVM style with the following key settings:

Setting Value IndentWidth 4 ColumnLimit 190 NamespaceIndentation All BreakBeforeBraces Custom (Attach style) AlwaysBreakTemplateDeclarations Yes Include order System headers first, then project headers

Run clang-format before committing:

clang-format -i <file>

docs.title: Naming conventions (.clang-tidy)
docs.text:
All identifiers use lower_case except where noted:

Identifier kind Case Prefix Classes and structs lower_case Functions lower_case Parameters lower_case p_ Local variables lower_case v_ Member variables lower_case m_ Static local variables lower_case v_ Enum constants UPPER_CASE Macros UPPER_CASE

Short loop indices (i, j, k, idx, it, iter) are exempt from the v_ prefix rule.

docs.title: Active check categories
docs.text:
The clang-tidy configuration enables a focused subset of checks:

  • bugprone-* for common bug patterns, with a targeted exclusion list
  • modernize-* for modern C++ idioms (trailing return types and a few others are excluded)
  • performance-* for performance anti-patterns
  • readability-* for identifier naming, redundant code, and general clarity
  • Selected rules from cert-*, cppcoreguidelines-*, misc-*, and hicpp-*

docs.title: Running lint locally
docs.text: The repository ships a scripts/lint.sh helper that runs the same checks CI does. You need clang-format and clang-tidy installed, plus CMake and the project dependencies so that a build can be configured to generate compile_commands.json.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Run both clang-format (check) and clang-tidy
bash scripts/lint.sh

# Check formatting only
bash scripts/lint.sh --format-only

# Run static analysis only
bash scripts/lint.sh --tidy-only

# Apply clang-format changes and clang-tidy fixes in place
bash scripts/lint.sh --fix

# Control parallelism (defaults to nproc)
bash scripts/lint.sh --jobs 4

docs.title: Environment overrides
docs.text:
If your system has versioned binaries (e.g. clang-format-21), the script picks the highest available version automatically. You can also pin them explicitly:

Variable Default Purpose CLANG_FORMAT auto-detected clang-format Path to the clang-format binary CLANG_TIDY auto-detected clang-tidy Path to the clang-tidy binary RUN_CLANG_TIDY auto-detected run-clang-tidy Path to the run-clang-tidy helper BUILD_DIR <repo>/.build-lint CMake build directory for compile_commands.json 
CLANG_FORMAT=clang-format-22 CLANG_TIDY=clang-tidy-22 bash scripts/lint.sh

The first time the tidy step runs it configures CMake in .build-lint/ to produce compile_commands.json. Subsequent runs reuse that directory, so the configuration step is skipped unless you delete it.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text:
Workflows are split by trigger: ci-*.yml runs on pull requests, except those that change only documentation, and on pushes to main and release, while release-*.yml runs on version tags (v*). Reusable building blocks (_build-*.yml) are shared so the tag-time publish reuses the exact build path CI exercises. The CI pipelines run in parallel:

Pipeline Runner Ubuntu 24.04 ubuntu-24.04 Windows 2025 windows-2025 macOS 26 macos-26 Java ubuntu-24.04, windows-2025, macos-26 Lint ubuntu-24.04

The macOS pipeline and the Java macOS jobs run on GitHub's hosted Apple Silicon runner, whose minutes come out of the account's monthly allowance. So they run only on pull requests into and pushes to main or release, on tags, and by hand: gh workflow run ci-cpp-macos.yml --ref <branch>.

The C++ build pipelines install dependencies (hwloc, Boost, spdlog, fmt, GoogleTest/GMock, and the platform MPI — OpenMPI on Linux and macOS, MS-MPI via MSYS2 on Windows), build gempba with the MPI component (-DGEMPBA_BUILD_MPI=ON), then run the full test suite via CTest; on Ubuntu that includes the multi-rank MPI integration tests under mpiexec. Each PR also builds the gempba-examples tree, the multithreading and the MPI examples, against an installed copy of the library, so the install / gempbaConfig.cmake / exported-headers chain is exercised on every change. On Ubuntu, one more job installs gempba without MPI and builds a consumer that compiles gempba::mpi against MPICH. A JUnit XML report is published as a workflow artifact after each run.

The Lint pipeline runs clang-format-22 (format check) and clang-tidy-22 (static analysis) against all first-party sources.

On a version tag (v*), the release-*.yml workflows build and publish packages of the core and the MPI component for every platform:

  • Ubuntu: .deb packages (libgempba-dev, libgempba-mpi-dev) published to a GPG-signed APT repository on GitHub Pages
  • Windows: MSYS2 packages (.pkg.tar.zst) attached to the GitHub Release
  • macOS: Homebrew formulae (gempba, gempba-mpi) pushed to the project's tap — built and brew test-ed on a real macOS runner first, so a non-installable formula blocks the release
  • Java: the gempba and gempba-mpi JARs, uploaded to Maven Central

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Working example programs live in the sibling repository rapastranac/gempba-examples. They consume GemPBA via find_package(gempba) exactly as a downstream user would, so they double as templates: find the closest one to your use case, swap in your algorithm, and go.

The tree is split by how a program runs: multithreading/src/ uses the core alone, and multiprocessing/src/ links the MPI component, gempba::mpi. To build them, install GemPBA (see Installation) and build the example repo against it. The MPI examples need the MPI component installed; configure with -DGEMPBA_EXAMPLES_MPI=OFF to build only the multithreading ones.

Java examples

Java/Maven equivalents live in rapastranac/gempba-java-examples, organized into mutithreading/ (the repository's spelling), multiprocessing/, and sequential/ Maven modules.
