Build

  • Test executable renamed from all_tests.out to all_tests (drops the Linux-style suffix so the same target name works on Windows)

docs.title: v2.0.0
docs.text:
August 17, 2025

GitHub ↗

Major release: new gempba::score, gempba::task_packet, and gempba::result public types replace string-based transport and the int reference value, alongside a sweeping clang-tidy rename of the public API (BranchHandler → branch_handler, MPI_Scheduler → mpi_scheduler, SchedulerParent → scheduler_parent, etc.).

Breaking changes

  • gempba::BranchHandler → gempba::branch_handler; getInstance() → get_instance(); try_push_MT → try_push_mt; member methods renamed per .clang-tidy (e.g. refValue() is gone — use get_score().get<T>())
  • gempba::MPI_Scheduler → gempba::mpi_scheduler; gempba::MPI_SchedulerCentralized → gempba::mpi_centralized_scheduler (header MPI_Scheduler_Centralized.hpp → mpi_centralized_scheduler.hpp)
  • gempba::SchedulerParent → gempba::scheduler_parent; fetchSolution() → fetch_solution() now returns task_packet instead of std::string; fetchResVec() → fetch_result_vector() returns std::vector<gempba::result> instead of std::vector<std::pair<int, std::string>>; push() now takes a task_packet&& instead of std::string
  • branch_handler::set_score / get_score / set_goal and the gempba::result constructor: int reference value replaced with gempba::score. set_goal now takes a gempba::goal enum plus gempba::score_type (was a bool)
  • hold_solution removed — replaced by try_update_result(solution, score): type-safe, parameters reordered, default parameter dropped, returns bool indicating whether the update happened
  • update_reference_value → try_update_reference_value; further renamed to try_update_reference_value_and_invalidate_result to reflect that it now clears any cached result when the score changes
  • score::get_loose removed — use score::to_string (logs print the value with its real underlying type) or the typed score::get<T>() accessor
  • set_ref_val_strategy_lookup → scheduler_parent::set_goal; lookup_strategy parameter → goal enum
  • EMPTY_RESULT constant removed — use result::EMPTY
  • m_reference_value member of gempba::result renamed to m_score; scheduler members m_ref_value_global → m_global_reference_value (and corresponding communicator member)
  • Examples no longer accept the THREADS_PER_TASK argument on the command line
  • GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING is now a value macro (0/1), no longer a bare definition — examples and downstream consumers must use #if GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING instead of #ifdef

Added

  • gempba::task_packet (include/utils/ipc/task_packet.hpp) — raw-byte transport that replaces serialized std::string in the scheduler API; serializers now return task_packet
  • gempba::result (include/utils/ipc/result.hpp) — bundles a score plus task_packet for shipping solutions between ranks
  • gempba::score (include/utils/ipc/score.hpp) and gempba::score_type enum (I32, I64, F32, F64, F128) — multi-primitive score support, formerly the integer-only reference_value (suggested by @Manuel-GithubAccount in #29)
  • gempba::goal enum to replace the previous boolean min/max strategy flag
  • score::make factory and score::to_string for type-aware logging
  • README "Concepts" section documenting goal, score, and score_type

Changed

  • Schedulers now exchange raw bytes (task_packet) instead of serialized strings end-to-end through branch_handler and scheduler_parent
  • mpi_scheduler and mpi_centralized_scheduler made structurally parallel: shared should_broadcast logic, utils::diff_time adopted in both, analogous global-reference-value checks
  • handle_full_messaging → monitor_and_notify_center_status
  • Most GEMPBA_DEBUG_COMMENTS macro sites replaced with a single utility method
  • README updated for all renamed identifiers and the new try_update_result / score usage
  • batch.sh → run.sh

Fixed

  • Communicator probing in mpi_centralized_scheduler (matching the fix already in mpi_scheduler)
  • openmpi invocation now binds processes to the intended number of cores
  • A try_update_result path that wasn't actually updating the stored reference value
  • GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING checks (#49): switched from #ifdef to #if, and the macro is now injected as an explicit 0/1 value so non-MP examples see it defined as false rather than undefined

Build

  • CMakeLists.txt project version bumped to 2.0.0
  • examples/CMakeLists.txt: defines GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING=1 for mp_* examples and GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING=0 for the rest (previously only the mp_* side was defined)

docs.title: v1.1.0
docs.text:
August 4, 2025

GitHub ↗

Citation metadata, a refreshed README, and dependency-management changes that consumers need to mirror.

The git tag is v.1.1.0 (extra dot — original spelling preserved). Everywhere else the version is referred to as v1.1.0.

Added

  • CITATION.cff and CITATION.bib at the repo root for academic citation
  • README sections for Requirements, Platforms, Dependency Management, Copyright and citing
  • FUNCTION_ARGS tag for routing serialized function arguments separately from other messages
  • REFERENCE_VAL_PROPOSAL and REFERENCE_VAL_UPDATE tags (split from the former single reference-value tag)

Changed

  • Inter-process tags in MPI_Modules/MPI_Scheduler.hpp are now an enum tags { ... } (CENTER_NODE, RUNNING_STATE, ASSIGNED_STATE, AVAILABLE_STATE, TERMINATION, REFERENCE_VAL_PROPOSAL, REFERENCE_VAL_UPDATE, NEXT_PROCESS, HAS_RESULT, NO_RESULT, FUNCTION_ARGS) replacing the previous #define macros (STATE_RUNNING, STATE_ASSIGNED, STATE_AVAILABLE, TERMINATION_TAG, REFVAL_UPDATE_TAG, NEXT_PROCESS_TAG, HAS_RESULT_TAG, NO_RESULT_TAG); consumers relying on the old macro names must rename to the enum values
  • README installation walkthrough moved above the description; CMake snippet now sets GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING, GEMPBA_DEBUG_COMMENTS, GEMPBA_BUILD_EXAMPLES, GEMPBA_BUILD_TESTS cache variables and links gempba::gempba

Fixed

  • examples/include/VertexCover.hpp include switched from fmt/core.h to <format> (matches the C++20 toolchain)

Build

  • CMake project version bumped to 1.1.0
  • spdlog removed from core CMake: find_package(spdlog REQUIRED) and spdlog::spdlog link are gone; consumers add it via CPM in external/CMakeLists.txt (pinned to gabime/spdlog@1.15.1, built static)

docs.title: v1.0.2
docs.text:
June 7, 2025

GitHub ↗

Easier external integration: GemPBA is now a consumable CMake library with a gempba::gempba target, a hook to inject a custom initial process topology, and CPM-based dependency fetch.

Added

  • gempba::gempba ALIAS target so consumers can target_link_libraries(... gempba::gempba)
  • SchedulerParent::set_custom_initial_topology(tree&&) to inject a custom initial process topology
  • New CMake options GEMPBA_BUILD_TESTS and GEMPBA_BUILD_EXAMPLES (default OFF when used as a subproject)
  • New CMake options GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING and GEMPBA_DEBUG_COMMENTS to drive compile-time macros from the build
  • wall_time, diff_time, shift_left utility functions in utils/utils.hpp
  • build_topology extracted from MPI_Scheduler into utils/utils.hpp
  • Public tree type at include/utils/tree.hpp (replaces MPI_Modules/Tree.hpp)
  • README section documenting CPM-based integration into a downstream project
  • Filename is now included in "file not found" exception messages

Changed

  • GemPBA now builds as a CMake library; examples and tests are separate subprojects gated by the new options
  • Public include roots are ${workspace}/include and ${workspace}/GemPBA, exported via target_include_directories (BUILD_INTERFACE)
  • Macro renames: MULTIPROCESSING_ENABLED → GEMPBA_MULTIPROCESSING; DEBUG_COMMENTS → GEMPBA_DEBUG_COMMENTS (consumers must update guards and target_compile_definitions)
  • BranchHandler API renamed to snake_case: setLookupStrategy → set_lookup_strategy, setLoadBalancingStrategy → set_load_balancing_strategy, getLoadBalancingStrategy → get_load_balancing_strategy
  • Enum types renamed: LookupStrategy → lookup_strategy, LoadBalancingStrategy → load_balancing_strategy (enumerator names like MAXIMISE, MINIMISE, QUASI_HORIZONTAL are unchanged)
  • scheduler_parent.hpp now includes <mpi.h> (was mpi/mpi.h); fixes builds on MPI distributions that don't expose the mpi/ prefix
  • argparse is now fetched via CPM instead of FetchContent_Declare
  • Verbose spdlog::info calls in production code demoted to spdlog::debug
  • Project version bumped to 1.0.2; release built against C++23 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23)
  • Default build type is Debug when GemPBA is the root project, inherited from the parent otherwise
  • README rewritten with shields.io markdown badges; licence and version badges fixed

Removed

  • Boost (system, serialization, fiber) is no longer linked or required by the library target; consumers no longer need to provide it
  • GTest is no longer required to build the library; it is now only needed when GEMPBA_BUILD_TESTS=ON
  • Legacy headers GemPBA/MPI_Modules/Tree.hpp, GemPBA/utils/Queue.hpp, GemPBA/utils/utils.hpp (replaced by their counterparts under include/utils/)

Fixed

  • Source-file detection in the root CMakeLists.txt
  • Hard-coded -O0 debug flags and add_definitions(-DDEBUG_COMMENTS) no longer leak into Release builds; flags are now per-configuration via generator expressions

Build

  • clang-tidy and clang-format configurations added at the repo root
  • .vs/ and CMakeSettings.json added to .gitignore

docs.title: v1.0.1
docs.text:
October 30, 2024

GitHub ↗

Restructured layout, C++23 build, typed strategy enums, and a scheduler base class so the semicentralized and centralized schedulers can coexist.

Added

  • gempba::SchedulerParent (MPI_Modules/scheduler_parent.hpp) — common abstract base for MPI_Scheduler and the centralized scheduler so both can be instantiated independently
  • gempba::ResultHolderParent (Resultholder/ResultHolderParent.hpp) — non-template base for ResultHolder so virtual interfaces no longer leak template parameters
  • gempba::LoadBalancingStrategy enum (QUASI_HORIZONTAL, WORK_STEALING) and gempba::LookupStrategy enum (MAXIMISE, MINIMISE) in utils/gempba_utils.hpp
  • BranchHandler::setLoadBalancingStrategy / getLoadBalancingStrategy
  • BranchHandler::setLookupStrategy(gempba::LookupStrategy) — typed replacement for the string-keyword setter
  • BranchHandler::getWorldRank
  • DLB_Handler::getRoot(int threadId)
  • THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES file with CPTL credits (Apache 2.0)

Changed

  • C++ standard bumped to C++23 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23); minimum CMake bumped to 3.28
  • Project layout reorganized: per-example executables under bin/, examples and tests in dedicated trees, headers under GemPBA/utils/ (was GemPBA/Utils/)
  • Build now produces one executable per file under examples/; sources matching mp_* get -DMULTIPROCESSING_ENABLED automatically
  • The library is now built as a CMake target named gempba (was a single a.out executable)
  • MPI_ENABLED compile macro renamed to MULTIPROCESSING_ENABLED
  • R_SEARCH macro removed; load-balancing strategy is now a runtime enum on BranchHandler (so misuse becomes a compile error rather than a silent macro miss)
  • Centralized scheduler class renamed from GemPBA::MPI_Scheduler (in MPI_Scheduler_Centralized.hpp) to gempba::MPI_SchedulerCentralized, allowing both schedulers to be linked into the same binary
  • Public namespace renamed from GemPBA to gempba (all classes and free functions moved)
  • MPI_Scheduler::rank_me, elapsedTime, getWorldSize, tasksRecvd, tasksSent, nextProcess are now const; runNode signature changed to take std::function callbacks (no longer a templated lambda accepting a serializer)
  • SchedulerParent::getTotalRequests returns size_t (was double on the prior centralized scheduler)

docs.title: v1.0.0
docs.text:
April 8, 2024

GitHub ↗

Initial stable release of GemPBA — a generic message-passing branch-and-bound framework for distributed C++ workloads.

docs.title: Scheduler Topologies
docs.text:
GemPBA's MPI component ships two scheduler topologies. The default recommendation is SEMI_CENTRALIZED.

#include <gempba/mpi.hpp>

// Semi-centralized (recommended)
auto* semi = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(gempba::mpi::scheduler_topology::SEMI_CENTRALIZED);

// Centralized (for comparison)
auto* central = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(gempba::mpi::scheduler_topology::CENTRALIZED);

A program creates one of them. Either way, every rank calls scheduler::run, and rank 0 is the coordinator: it takes no part in the computation.

docs.title: What the coordinator does, and does not do
docs.text:
The coordinator (rank 0) has a single responsibility: knowing who is idle and assigning available workers to busy ones. It never holds tasks, never routes tasks, and never participates in computation.

Before the seed, the coordinator sends every worker its initial list of waiting processes: a binomial tree over ranks 1 to N-1, or the tree given to set_custom_initial_topology. From then on, a worker reports RUNNING_STATE when it starts and AVAILABLE_STATE when it runs out of work:

  • When a running worker has no waiting process, the coordinator gives it an available one.
  • When a worker becomes available, the coordinator assigns it to a running worker, chosen at random among those that have none waiting.

Each assignment reaches the busy worker as a NEXT_PROCESS message, and the next time that worker has a spare subtask, it sends it directly to the waiting process.

The critical consequence: tasks only travel to workers the coordinator has confirmed are idle. This eliminates the bounce-back problem that plagues decentralized strategies, where a task sent to a peer may arrive after that peer has already received work from somewhere else and must reject it, wasting a full round-trip.

docs.title: Communication model
docs.text: The coordinator never waits for a worker to query it: it pushes a message the moment a relevant state changes, a new best value or a worker assignment. Workers pick these messages up between tasks with a non-blocking probe (MPI_Iprobe), so they learn of an assignment without asking for one.

docs.title: Network topology
docs.text: Semi-centralized topology: the coordinator keeps statuses, assignments and the global best value and exchanges only signals and scores with the workers, while tasks travel directly from worker to worker Coordinator (rank 0) process statuses process assignments global best value Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 Worker N status · assignment score proposal · best value task (direct) task (direct) … seed task payload signal, no payload score Every task the coordinator never sees still gets its acknowledgement, which is how the run knows it is over.

docs.title: Protocol walkthrough
docs.text:
Semi-centralized protocol: the coordinator sends Worker 1 its waiting processes and the seed; workers report RUNNING_STATE and AVAILABLE_STATE, send tasks directly to the processes assigned to them, and acknowledge their parents once passive; when the coordinator's deficit reaches zero it sends TERMINATION to every worker Coordinator rank 0 Worker 1 rank 1 Worker 2 rank 2 Worker 3 rank 3 Every rank calls scheduler::run; rank 0 passes the seed NEXT_PROCESS [W2, W3]: its initial waiting processes seed task RUNNING_STATE task (direct) RUNNING_STATE task (direct) score proposal best value, to every worker W3's subtree is done TASK_RECEIVED: the deferred acknowledgement AVAILABLE_STATE NEXT_PROCESS [W3]: to a running worker with none waiting task (direct) Each rank acknowledges its parent once it is passive and every task it sent has been acknowledged TASK_RECEIVED TASK_RECEIVED TASK_RECEIVED deficit 0: the search is over TERMINATION: message counts and the run_outcome, to every worker

The heart of the strategy:

  1. Worker 1 starts the seed already knowing its waiting processes, W2 and W3, so it sends its first spare subtasks directly to them. The coordinator is not involved in the data transfer.
  2. When W3 runs out of work, it reports AVAILABLE_STATE. The coordinator assigns it to W2, a running worker with nobody waiting, with a NEXT_PROCESS signal: no task payload crosses the coordinator.
  3. W2 sends its next spare subtask to W3, and the cascade goes on.

Because the coordinator's status table is the single source of truth, and W3 was confirmed available before W2 sends to it, the task is always accepted. No bounce-back.

docs.title: How the run ends
docs.text:
Termination is exact: there is no timeout and no quiet period. Both topologies detect it with Dijkstra–Scholten acknowledgements:

  • Every task a rank sends, the seed included, raises that rank's deficit by one, and every acknowledgement (TASK_RECEIVED) lowers it.
  • A rank that receives a task while it has no parent makes the sender its parent, and holds that acknowledgement back. Any other task is acknowledged at once.
  • A rank acknowledges its parent only once it is passive, with no task left to run, and its deficit is zero. That clears its parent.
  • Rank 0 never takes a parent. So when its deficit reaches zero, every task ever sent has finished: the search is over, provably.

Rank 0 then sends TERMINATION to every worker. The message says how many score updates and assignments that worker should still expect, so each worker reads the ones in flight before it leaves, and it carries the run's run_outcome, so every rank returns the same answer from scheduler::run. A stop request travels on the same acknowledgements, so it reaches rank 0 before the deficit can reach zero (see Stopping a Run).

docs.title: Centralized
docs.text:
The coordinator is an active participant: it maintains a bounded task queue. Workers send their spare subtasks to it, and it dispatches them to available workers, highest priority first. The priority is a cheap proxy computed from the task's bytes: the number of set bits in the packet plus the runnable id.

The queue is bounded by compile-time limits: 1000 tasks per process, times the number of ranks, or 10 GB of memory. Past either one, the coordinator broadcasts CENTER_IS_FULL, and workers run their spare subtasks locally instead of sending them. Once the queue is back below 80% of the task limit and memory below 90%, it broadcasts CENTER_IS_FREE, and workers send again. The coordinator never rejects a task it has received: the backpressure happens before the send. Because branching algorithms are exponential, though, the queue saturates quickly in practice, and most tasks never enter it, which undermines the priority-based selection that is the approach's main advantage.

Centralized protocol: workers send their spare tasks to the coordinator, which queues them by priority and dispatches them to available workers; past its limits it broadcasts CENTER_IS_FULL and workers run their tasks locally until CENTER_IS_FREE; it never rejects a task, and ends the run once its deficit is zero and its queue empty Coordinator rank 0 Worker 1 rank 1 Worker 2 rank 2 Worker 3 rank 3 seed task RUNNING_STATE task for the coordinator TASK_RECEIVED queued by priority task from the coordinator, highest priority first RUNNING_STATE more tasks … past 1000 × ranks tasks or 10 GB CENTER_IS_FULL, to every worker workers run their spare tasks locally; nothing is rejected or sent back below 80% of the tasks and 90% of memory CENTER_IS_FREE, to every worker task from the coordinator Workers acknowledge their parents once passive, as in semi-centralized deficit 0 and queue empty TERMINATION, to every worker

At small process counts the centralized topology performs comparably to semi-centralized. At scale, the coordinator becomes the bottleneck: every task handoff, regardless of which two workers are involved, must traverse the coordinator twice (inbound + outbound). This is the behavior the semi-centralized design was built to avoid.

The centralized scheduler ends the run the same way, once its deficit is zero and its queue is empty. It ignores set_custom_initial_topology, since no task goes from worker to worker.

The centralized scheduler is kept in the library for reproducing the paper's comparison experiments and benchmarking custom scheduling strategies.

docs.title: Decentralized
docs.text:
Not available in GemPBA

This topology is not implemented in the library. It is described here as background so the design choices of the semi-centralized strategy can be understood in context.

There is no central coordinator. Available cores are organized into a core-tree: the parent of core r is r − 2⌊log2 r⌋, so the root holds the full initial instance and each core requests work from its parent when it becomes idle. If the parent has a pending task it sends the highest-priority sub-instance from its own search tree; if it has nothing, the request fails and the child must retry with a different ancestor.

Decentralized core-tree, not in GemPBA: core r's parent is r minus the largest power of two not above r; parents send tasks down and children send work requests up, which may fail Core 0 (root) Core 1 Core 2 Core 4 Core 3 Core 5 Core 6 Core 7 task (parent → child) work request; may fail

Advantages over centralized: no single routing bottleneck; no synchronization needed; communication overhead is low since cores never route through a shared queue.

Drawbacks:

  • Failed work requests. A core's view of its parent's availability is stale. By the time a request arrives, the parent may have already sent its last task elsewhere; the request fails and the core wastes a full round-trip retrying. Under difficult graphs this accounts for a large fraction of total communication.
  • Skewed core-tree. The root has ~log c neighbours while most leaves have none. Subtrees at leaf cores rarely receive help; the root's subtree is over-assisted.
  • No global best value. Each core tracks only its local best, which may lag the true global optimum and fail to prune branches as aggressively as a globally informed worker could.
  • No global task priority. A core picks the highest-priority task in its own subtree, not across the whole search space.

How semi-centralized addresses both extremes:

GemPBA's semi-centralized topology removes the bottleneck of the centralized approach and the failed-request / stale-view problems of the decentralized approach:

Centralized Decentralized Semi-centralized Coordinator bottleneck Yes No No Tasks traverse coordinator Yes No No Global best value Yes Partial Yes Spare tasks kept local Yes, while the queue is full No No Request failures No Yes No Task priority Queue-limited Local only Global

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Semi-Centralized Centralized Coordinator role Assigns idle workers to busy ones Active task router Task path Worker → Worker (direct) Worker → Coordinator → Worker Coordinator sends Lightweight assignment signals Full task payloads Communication model Push-based Queue and dispatch, with full/free backpressure Bounce-back Eliminated None: a full coordinator stops the sends instead Termination Exact: Dijkstra–Scholten acknowledgements Exact: acknowledgements, once the queue is empty Coordinator bottleneck No Yes, at scale Recommended for Production Benchmarking

docs.title: Stopping a Run
docs.text: A run usually ends when the search space is exhausted. From gempba v5.0.0 you can also stop it early and keep the best result found so far, and the run says how it ended.

docs.title: How a run ends
docs.text:
A run ends in one of three ways:

End What happened The result Completed The whole search space was explored. Proven. Interrupted A stop ended the run early. The stop came from a signal (SIGINT or SIGTERM), from the stop call in your code, or from the dashboard. The best one found before the stop, not a proven one. Lost The run was killed without warning: SIGKILL, a crash or a node failure. None: the program dies before returning one.

A completed or interrupted run says how it ended, as Reading how it ended shows. A lost run can't, and that silence is what tells you it was lost.

docs.title: What a stop does
docs.text:
• From the stop on, nodes that haven't started are pruned. Nodes already running finish their own work, and the run then returns its best result so far.
  • Under MPI, every rank stops, even ranks that saw no signal. A worker that sees the stop tells the root, and the root tells every worker. Every rank returns the same outcome.
  • The first stop wins, whatever triggered it, until gempba::shutdown(). Later stops change nothing.
  • A stop doesn't cut a node short. If one node runs for a long time, poll gempba::stop_requested() (Java: GemPBA.isStopRequested()) inside it and return early once it's true.

docs.title: With a signal
docs.text:
Signals stop the run gracefully by default. create_node_manager takes SIGINT and SIGTERM, and shutdown gives them back:

  • Ctrl+C (SIGINT) once stops the run gracefully. A second Ctrl+C kills the process, in case the wind-down takes too long. In Java, the second one goes to the JVM's own handler, which shuts the JVM down as usual.
  • SIGTERM stops the run gracefully, and further SIGTERMs don't kill it. This is the signal a batch scheduler sends, so a job that hits its time limit ends interrupted rather than lost; see On a Slurm cluster.
  • In C++, gempba takes only a signal that nothing handles yet. If your program installed its own handler first, gempba leaves the signal to it, and that signal won't stop the run gracefully.

To keep the signals' default behavior, which kills the process, turn this off. Call it before create_node_manager to keep gempba from taking them, or later to give them back at once:

gempba::stop_on_signals(false);

GemPBA.stopOnSignals(false);

docs.title: From your code
docs.text:
Call the stop from any thread, for example from a watchdog that enforces a time budget. It returns at once:

#include <gempba/gempba.hpp>

gempba::request_stop();                 // stop the run, from any thread

if (gempba::stop_requested()) {         // inside a long node: return early
    return;
}

import io.gempba.GemPBA;

GemPBA.requestStop();                   // stop the run, from any thread

if (GemPBA.isStopRequested()) {         // inside a long node: return early
    return;
}

stop_requested() stays true from the first stop, by any trigger, until shutdown().

docs.title: From the dashboard
docs.text:
A telemetry client can stop the run with the stop control line on the dashboard socket. The GemPBA Dashboard's Stop the run sends it, from the dashboard's next release (2.1); 2.0 has no stop. Because any user on the host can reach that socket, the line carries a token, and the run stops only when the token matches the GEMPBA_STOP_TOKEN environment variable the run was started with:

export GEMPBA_STOP_TOKEN=pick-your-own   # set before starting the program

{"kind":"stop","token":"pick-your-own"}

A run started without GEMPBA_STOP_TOKEN refuses every stop line, and a stop line with another token is refused too. Each refusal logs a warning:

telemetry: refused a stop line: this run has no GEMPBA_STOP_TOKEN
telemetry: refused a stop line with the wrong token

The example repositories' cluster jobs export GEMPBA_STOP_TOKEN=${GEMPBA_STOP_TOKEN:-s3cret}, so their runs take a stop line out of the box. The token you set in your own environment overrides that default.

docs.title: In code
docs.text:
Under MPI, scheduler::run returns how the run ended, the same on every rank:

const gempba::run_outcome outcome = scheduler->run(nm, runnables, std::move(seed));

if (outcome.m_reason == gempba::end_reason::INTERRUPTED) {
    // the result is the best one found before the stop, not a proven one
}
Field Values m_reason end_reason::COMPLETED or end_reason::INTERRUPTED m_trigger stop_trigger::NONE for a completed run; otherwise CODE (request_stop()), SIGNAL (SIGINT or SIGTERM) or CONTROL (a stop line) m_signal The signal's number when m_trigger is SIGNAL; 0 otherwise

In Java, Scheduler.run returns the same thing as an io.gempba.value.RunOutcome record, with reason() (EndReason), trigger() (StopTrigger), signal() and isInterrupted():

RunOutcome outcome = sched.run(nm, runnables, seed, seedRunnableId);

if (outcome.isInterrupted()) {
    // the result is the best one found before the stop, not a proven one
}

A multithreading run has no scheduler, so nothing returns an outcome. Check gempba::stop_requested() (Java: GemPBA.isStopRequested()) after the wait and before shutdown(): true means a stop cut the run short.

docs.title: In the log
docs.text:
gempba logs one line when the run ends: under MPI the root rank logs it when scheduler::run returns, and a multithreading run logs it at shutdown(). A completed run logs at info:

gempba: run completed: the whole search space was explored, so the result is proven

An interrupted run logs a warning that names what stopped it:

gempba: run interrupted by SIGTERM: the result is the best one found before the stop, not a proven one
Stopped by The warning says Ctrl+C run interrupted by SIGINT (Ctrl+C) SIGTERM run interrupted by SIGTERM The stop call run interrupted by gempba::request_stop(), from Java's GemPBA.requestStop() too The dashboard run interrupted from the dashboard, after telemetry: a dashboard client stopped the run

docs.title: On the telemetry stream
docs.text:
At shutdown the aggregator sends a final line, marked "final":true, then closes the connection. That line says how the run ended in end:

"end":{"reason":"interrupted","trigger":"signal","signal":"SIGTERM"}
  • reason is "completed" or "interrupted".
  • An interrupted run adds trigger: "code", "signal" or "control".
  • A stop by signal adds signal, its name, such as "SIGINT" or "SIGTERM".

A multithreading run has no scheduler, so its end comes from whether a stop was requested: "completed", or "interrupted" with the stop's trigger. Under MPI, end is absent when the scheduler didn't report how the run ended, for example when it threw. A connection that closes without a final line was lost. The full field reference is in gempba's wire-format.md; Data model maps it.

docs.title: On a Slurm cluster
docs.text:
When a job reaches its time limit, Slurm sends SIGTERM to the job's processes, then SIGKILL once the cluster's KillWait has passed, often 30 seconds. gempba takes that SIGTERM as a stop, but the run has only those seconds to wind down. If its running nodes take longer, the job is killed and the run is lost.

Ask Slurm to send SIGTERM earlier with --signal, giving the run time to end interrupted, with its best result, its log line and its final telemetry line:

#SBATCH --signal=TERM@<seconds>   # SIGTERM <seconds> before the time limit
  • Choose <seconds> longer than your longest node takes to finish. Slurm may send the signal up to 60 seconds earlier than asked.
  • Launch the program with srun, as the examples do, so the signal reaches every rank. Leave out the B: prefix: --signal=B:TERM@… signals only the batch script's shell, not the program.

To stop a running job gracefully by hand, send it SIGTERM alone instead of cancelling it outright:

scancel --signal=TERM <jobid>

docs.title: Writing your own scheduler
docs.text: A custom scheduler takes part in the stop too: it polls gempba::stop_requested(), tells the other ranks, and returns the same run_outcome from do_run on every rank. gempba's custom-schedulers.md lists what it must do.

docs.title: Why GemPBA
docs.text:
If you have ever tried to parallelize a branch-and-bound algorithm by hand, you already know the pain. You start with a clean recursive function, it works great, and then someone says "can we use all these CPU cores?" Suddenly you are drowning in thread pools, work queues, mutexes protecting a shared best-solution, and recursive calls that somehow need to coordinate across threads without stomping on each other.

GemPBA was built because the same problem kept appearing from scratch for every new branching algorithm. The scheduling scaffold was always the same; only the algorithm in the middle changed. And every time an existing library appeared as a candidate, either no one could figure out how to build it (the documentation was three paragraphs and a "see the tests"), or it was so tightly coupled to one algorithm structure that adapting it meant basically rewriting it.

GemPBA's answer to this is a framework that inserts itself into your recursion through a small set of parameter additions. You keep writing your algorithm the way you always have. GemPBA handles the rest.

Distributed, it also gets a hard part right that hand-rolled schedulers usually guess at: knowing when the search is over. GemPBA's MPI schedulers detect termination exactly, with Dijkstra–Scholten acknowledgements rather than a timeout, so a run never ends with work still in flight and never idles waiting out a quiet period (How the run ends). And when you need it to end sooner, a stop winds it down gracefully, and the run tells you whether its result is proven or the best found so far (Stopping a Run).

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Pick the path that fits your situation:

  • Requirements — what you need before building or installing
  • Installation — install a pre-built package (APT, MSYS2, Homebrew, or Maven for Java), or embed GemPBA in your project via CPM
  • Building — build from source with CMake
  • Quick Start — minimal working example: parallelize your first branching algorithm
  • Java — the same core from the JVM, from Maven Central

docs.title: Building from Source
docs.text:
Build from source when a pre-built package is not an option — custom configure flags, an unsupported distro, or contributing back. For everyday use, prefer a pre-built package.

First install the build dependencies for your platform.

docs.title: Ubuntu / macOS
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/rapastranac/gempba.git
cd gempba
cmake -B build                               # compiles the MPI component too; -DGEMPBA_BUILD_MPI=OFF needs no MPI
cmake --build build --parallel
sudo cmake --install build                   # optional: install system-wide

docs.title: Windows (MSYS2 / UCRT64)
docs.text:
Open an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell, then:

git clone https://github.com/rapastranac/gempba.git
cd gempba
cmake -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build --parallel

Either way, the install ships the MPI component as source, so find_package(gempba COMPONENTS mpi) works against it once MPI is on the machine. GEMPBA_BUILD_MPI only decides whether this build compiles the component too, which gempba's own tests and the Java binding need.

docs.title: CMake flags
docs.text:
When GemPBA is the root project (you cloned and built it directly), it defaults to a developer build: the MPI component, hwloc and the tests are on, and with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE the build is Debug. As a subproject (pulled in via CPM/add_subdirectory), every flag defaults to OFF and you opt in to what you need.

Flag Root default Description GEMPBA_BUILD_MPI ON Compile the MPI component, gempba::mpi, in this build; needs MPI. The install ships its source either way GEMPBA_HWLOC ON Use hwloc for the hardware-topology probe (telemetry) GEMPBA_BUILD_TESTS ON Build the GoogleTest suite GEMPBA_MPI_INTEGRATION_TESTS OFF Register the multi-rank MPI tests with CTest, which runs them under mpiexec; needs GEMPBA_BUILD_TESTS and GEMPBA_BUILD_MPI GEMPBA_DEBUG_COMMENTS OFF Extra runtime logging GEMPBA_BUILD_JAVA_BINDING OFF Build the Java JNI shared library (requires a JDK and -DGEMPBA_JNI_CLASSIFIER=<os>-<arch>)

Pass any flag at configure time:

cmake -B build -DGEMPBA_BUILD_MPI=OFF -DGEMPBA_HWLOC=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

Tests and the MPI component

The MPI component's unit tests build only with GEMPBA_BUILD_MPI=ON; without it, the suite runs the core's tests alone.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text: ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

docs.title: Running examples
docs.text: Example programs no longer live in the gempba source tree — they moved to the sibling repository rapastranac/gempba-examples (C++) and rapastranac/gempba-java-examples (Java), where they consume GemPBA via find_package(gempba) exactly as a downstream user would. Clone one of those repos, install GemPBA (or point it at your build), and build the examples from there. See the Examples page for the catalog.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
GemPBA is one library with multithreading built in, plus an optional MPI component:

  • The core (gempba) uses all the cores of a single machine. No MPI to install, nothing to configure. If you are unsure, start here.
  • The MPI component (gempba-mpi, the same name as the Java artifact) adds the schedulers that distribute work across multiple machines/nodes over MPI. Install it on top of the core when one machine is not enough. It installs as source: your build compiles it against the MPI on your machine (Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI), so one installation works with any of them.

A program uses the MPI component only when it asks for it (see Using in your CMake project), so multithreading and MPI programs build side by side from the same installation.

docs.title: Ubuntu 24.04 (APT)
docs.text:
The .deb packages are built for Ubuntu 24.04 (noble) and live in a signed APT repository hosted at https://rapastranac.github.io/gempba. The repository serves the latest release; older .debs stay attached to each GitHub Release. Register the repository and its signing key once per machine, then install:

# 1. Trust the GemPBA signing key (one-time)
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://rapastranac.github.io/gempba/gempba-archive-keyring.gpg \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/gempba.gpg > /dev/null

# 2. Register the repository (one-time)
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/gempba.gpg] https://rapastranac.github.io/gempba noble main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gempba.list > /dev/null
sudo apt update

# 3. Install
sudo apt install libgempba-dev          # the core
sudo apt install libgempba-mpi-dev      # the MPI component, as source; with libopenmpi-dev or libmpich-dev

libgempba-mpi-dev Depends: libgempba-dev of the same version, plus libopenmpi-dev (≥ 4.0) or libmpich-dev. Ubuntu 24.04's MPICH package starts every rank of a job alone (Launchpad bug 2072338), so use Open MPI there.

If you already have the repository registered and just want to pick up a new release:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade libgempba-dev libgempba-mpi-dev

Alternatively, download the .debs directly from the Releases page and install them manually:

sudo dpkg -i libgempba-dev_<version>_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i libgempba-mpi-dev_<version>_amd64.deb   # the MPI component, if you need it

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text: dpkg -s libgempba-dev | grep -E "Status|Version"

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
sudo apt remove libgempba-dev libgempba-mpi-dev

Use purge instead of remove to also clear any leftover configuration files.

docs.title: Windows (MSYS2 / UCRT64)
docs.text:
GemPBA is in MSYS2's own UCRT64 repository. Install it from an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell:

pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba       # the core
pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba-mpi   # the MPI component, as source; brings the core and MS-MPI

pacman -Syu picks up new releases with the rest of your system.

Each GitHub Release also carries the .pkg.tar.zst files, for a specific version or before MSYS2 has picked a release up. Their names carry the version, such as mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba-5.0.0-1-any.pkg.tar.zst; install them with pacman -U:

pacman -U mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba-<version>-any.pkg.tar.zst       # the core
pacman -U mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba-mpi-<version>-any.pkg.tar.zst   # the MPI component, as source

Prefer to build from the PKGBUILD instead, in the same shell:

curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rapastranac/gempba/main/packaging/msys2/PKGBUILD
MINGW_ARCH=ucrt64 makepkg-mingw -si

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text: pacman -Qi mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
pacman -R mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba-mpi   # the MPI component, if installed
pacman -R mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gempba       # the core

docs.title: macOS (Homebrew)
docs.text:
Install from the project's Homebrew tap:

brew tap rapastranac/gempba
brew install gempba       # the core
brew install gempba-mpi   # the MPI component, as source; installs gempba too
brew install open-mpi     # or mpich: the MPI your build compiles it against

docs.title: Java (Maven)
docs.text: GemPBA is also a Maven dependency: io.github.rapastranac:gempba, or gempba-mpi for MPI, on Maven Central. See the dedicated Java section for the dependency snippet, which MPI the JAR needs, and a full Quick Start.

docs.title: Using in your CMake project (find_package)
docs.text:
Once GemPBA is installed system-wide, wire it into your project. Ask for the core, and for the MPI component when a program uses MPI:

find_package(gempba REQUIRED)                  # gempba::gempba, the core
find_package(gempba REQUIRED COMPONENTS mpi)   # adds gempba::mpi, compiled here against the MPI CMake finds

target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE gempba::gempba)
target_link_libraries(my_mpi_app PRIVATE gempba::mpi)   # brings gempba::gempba and MPI with it

libgempba is a shared library that keeps its own dependencies (spdlog, fmt, hwloc) inside, so a consumer needs only the C++ standard library, plus MPI for gempba::mpi. gempba::mpi is compiled in your build with your compiler, which must be compatible with the one that built libgempba, as for any C++ code that uses it. Each build directory compiles it against the MPI CMake finds there, so switching between MPIs takes another build directory, not a reinstall.

docs.title: Multithreading and MPI programs
docs.text:
The API is the same for every program. A multithreading program creates its load balancer and node manager from <gempba/gempba.hpp> alone:

#include <gempba/gempba.hpp>

auto* lb = gempba::create_load_balancer(gempba::QUASI_HORIZONTAL);
auto& nm = gempba::create_node_manager(lb);

An MPI program first creates its scheduler from <gempba/mpi.hpp>, then passes it to both:

#include <gempba/gempba.hpp>
#include <gempba/mpi.hpp>

auto* scheduler = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(gempba::mpi::SEMI_CENTRALIZED);
auto* lb = gempba::create_load_balancer(gempba::QUASI_HORIZONTAL, scheduler);
auto& nm = gempba::create_node_manager(lb, scheduler);

The core and the MPI component link into one program together. The Quick Start builds a complete multithreading program and lists what an MPI one adds.

docs.title: Embedding via CPM (source builds)
docs.text:
For a source-level integration, create external/CMakeLists.txt:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28)
include(FetchContent)

project(external)

set(CPM_DOWNLOAD_LOCATION "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/cmake/CPM.cmake")
if (NOT (EXISTS ${CPM_DOWNLOAD_LOCATION}))
    message(STATUS "Downloading CPM.cmake")
    file(DOWNLOAD https://github.com/cpm-cmake/CPM.cmake/releases/latest/download/CPM.cmake ${CPM_DOWNLOAD_LOCATION})
endif ()
include(${CPM_DOWNLOAD_LOCATION})

CPMAddPackage(
    NAME gempba
    GITHUB_REPOSITORY rapastranac/gempba
    GIT_TAG v5.0.0
)

add_library(external INTERFACE)
target_link_libraries(external INTERFACE gempba)

Then in your root CMakeLists.txt:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.28)

project(your-project VERSION 1.0 LANGUAGES CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23)

# GemPBA flags
set(GEMPBA_BUILD_MPI ON CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)        # compile gempba::mpi too (needs MPI); OFF builds the core alone
set(GEMPBA_HWLOC ON CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)            # hardware-topology probe (telemetry)
set(GEMPBA_DEBUG_COMMENTS OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)  # (Optional) extra logging
add_subdirectory(external)

add_executable(main main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(main PUBLIC gempba::mpi)      # gempba::gempba for a multithreading program

For ready-to-clone consumer projects, see the gempba-examples (C++) and gempba-java-examples (Java) repositories.

docs.title: GemPBA for Java
docs.text:
GemPBA's core is C++, for speed, and its Java API puts that same core in your JVM. It's on Maven Central, with no repository or token to configure:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.github.rapastranac</groupId>
  <artifactId>gempba</artifactId>        <!-- or gempba-mpi -->
  <version>5.0.0</version>
</dependency>

Write import io.gempba.* and call the same load balancers, node manager and schedulers you would from C++, from Java this time. If you have a JVM pipeline, a Spark job, an Airflow operator, or an enterprise application where C++ was the wrong language but you still wanted GemPBA's scheduler, this is the bridge.

On Maven Central from v5.0.0

The Java binding landed in v4.1.0. From v5.0.0 it's on Maven Central as io.github.rapastranac:gempba and gempba-mpi, in the io.gempba packages.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Natives inside the JAR. Each published JAR carries the native binaries for Linux, Windows, and macOS inside the artifact, under natives/<os>-<arch>/. A NativeLoader picks the right binary at runtime — no per-platform build dance, no classifier juggling, no LD_LIBRARY_PATH footnote. The same JAR runs unchanged on any supported platform.
  • Two artifacts, one API. Pick gempba (no MPI needed) or gempba-mpi (adds MPI schedulers, requires an MPI runtime on the host). The Java surface mirrors the C++ one: GemPBA.createLoadBalancer(...), GemPBA.createNodeManager(...), and so on.
  • Built on a C ABI. Underneath the JNI layer sits an extern "C" surface (<gempba/cabi/gempba.h>, and gempba_mpi.h for MPI) covering the full runtime. The Java binding is its first consumer; the same headers are what any future Python / Rust / .NET binding will sit on.

docs.title: Why you serialize arguments
docs.text:
C++ leans on templates to accept any task signature; Java can't, so the binding moves task arguments and results across the language boundary as bytes rather than typed values. You provide that translation as a Serializer / Deserializer pair when you seed the search — a small, honest tax for driving a native scheduler from the JVM.

In practice it is lighter than it sounds: on a single machine only the seed is serialized, because child nodes capture their arguments straight from the Java closure. See How it works for the full story — how GemPBA reuses its task_packet transport to make this work, and why the cost lands where it does.

docs.title: How the binding works
docs.text: GemPBA's scheduler, load balancer, and thread pool all run in native C++. The Java binding doesn't reimplement any of that — it is a typed front-end that calls into the native runtime and lets the runtime call back. The single idea that makes that round trip possible is a type GemPBA already had for an entirely different reason: task_packet.

docs.title: Bytes, not types
docs.text:
In C++, GemPBA leans on templates: your task can have any argument types, and the compiler bakes a concrete, fully typed function for each one. Java has no equivalent — generics are erased at runtime, and there is no way to synthesize a native call to fit arbitrary JVM types.

So the binding stops trying to move typed arguments across the language boundary and moves bytes instead. task_packet is the buffer those bytes ride in.

The elegant part is that this buffer was not invented for Java. GemPBA already used task_packet to ship a node's payload between MPI ranks, where work genuinely has to leave one process as raw bytes and be reconstructed in another. The Java binding simply reuses that same channel: whenever a task's argument or result crosses between the JVM and native code, it travels as a task_packet. Nothing about the transport is Java-specific — it's the same packet, pointed at a new destination.

docs.title: What crosses, and when
docs.text:
You supply two small functions when you seed the search — a Serializer (your argument → bytes) and a Deserializer (bytes → your argument). That pair is the only translation the binding needs.

  • Into native code. The seed's argument is serialized into a task_packet and handed to the runtime. When a worker thread later runs the task, the binding feeds the packet back through your Deserializer and calls your code.
  • Back out. A result that has to cross back travels as bytes too, reconstructed through a Deserializer on arrival.
  • Children stay home (multithreading). A child node created inside a running task captures its arguments in the Java closure — they're already on the JVM heap, so no packet is built. Only the seed makes the initial crossing.
  • Children travel (multiprocessing). When work is distributed across processes, a child may be dispatched to another rank — and there the task_packet does its original job, carrying the node's payload over the wire.

That asymmetry is the whole cost model: on one machine you pay the serialization tax once, for the seed; across machines you pay it wherever work actually moves — which is exactly where task_packet was always meant to be paid.

docs.title: The price in practice
docs.text:
So what does the serialization tax actually cost? Below is the same synthetic benchmark — a binary tree of depth 25 (33,554,432 leaves) with identical per-node work — run in C++ and in Java on one 24-core machine (no SMT). The multithreading runs use a single 24-thread pool; the multiprocessing runs use 7 MPI ranks (6 workers × 4 threads + 1 coordinator, semi-centralized) so both modes field the same 24 worker threads.

Mode Layout C++ Java Java vs C++ Multithreading 1 process × 24 threads 142.07 s 141.47 s −0.4 % (par) Multiprocessing 6 × 4 workers + 1 coordinator 201.76 s 214.29 s +6.2 %

All four runs returned the identical result — a leaf count of 33,554,432 — so each walked exactly the same tree. The time difference is binding overhead and nothing else.

The shape is what you would hope for. On a single machine the overhead vanishes into measurement noise — Java came in a hair ahead of C++ on this run, which is just another way of saying the two are indistinguishable. Across processes, where every task handed to another rank is genuinely serialized and shipped, the cost becomes visible but stays in single digits, around 6 %. You pay essentially nothing to stay on one machine, and a small, bounded premium for the one operation that inherently needs serialization: moving work between processes.

About these numbers

Single representative runs at depth 25 with the semi-centralized scheduler, on one host. Per-rank elapsed times were tightly clustered (the load was well balanced), and the workload is compute-heavy by design, so it reflects a realistic job rather than a micro-benchmark. Expect variation with per-node cost, topology, and hardware.

docs.title: The same code scales from one machine to many
docs.text:
Here is the part worth internalizing: the Serializer / Deserializer pair you write for the seed of a single-machine program is the same kind of code a distributed (gempba-mpi) program needs, because under the hood it is the same task_packet doing the same job, only travelling farther.

So the habit you build on day one is the habit that scales. When a problem outgrows one machine, you switch the dependency to gempba-mpi, create a scheduler with Mpi.createScheduler, give the children the same serializer pair the seed already has, register the task as a runnable, and call Scheduler.run on every rank under mpiexec. Your task logic, the recursion itself, stays as it is: going distributed is a small, mechanical change rather than a port, and, as the numbers above show, one that costs only a few percent. The Quick Start lists the four changes.

docs.text:
A JAR has to carry its native library compiled, so unlike the C++ packages, gempba-mpi is built against one MPI per OS: Open MPI on Linux and macOS, MS-MPI on Windows. With another MPI only, such as MPICH, Intel MPI or Cray MPICH, its native library fails to load, and the error names the MPI it needs.

To use another MPI, build the native library against it on Linux, from the tag of your gempba-mpi version so it matches the JAR's classes. It needs a C++23 compiler, CMake, curl, Maven, a JDK and your MPI on PATH; on a cluster, load their modules first. build_jar_host_linux.sh builds the static hwloc, fmt and spdlog the library links, builds it against that MPI, names the MPI it found, and installs the JAR into ~/.m2. Then pass the library with the gempba.native.path system property, which replaces the bundled one:

git clone --branch vVERSION https://github.com/rapastranac/gempba.git && cd gempba
bash scripts/build_jar_host_linux.sh MP
mpiexec -n 4 java -Dgempba.native.path=$PWD/bindings/java/src/main/resources/natives/linux-x86_64/gempba_jni.so -cp <classpath> <main class>

Intel Macs

The JARs' macOS native is for Apple Silicon only. On an Intel Mac, scripts/build_jar_macos.sh MT (or MP) builds natives/osx-x86_64/gempba_jni.dylib; pass it with -Dgempba.native.path.

docs.title: Quick Start (Java)
docs.text:
This walks through a complete multithreading program: a synthetic binary-tree traversal that counts leaves in parallel. It is a trimmed version of the synthetic_void example from gempba-java-examples, and it uses the public io.gempba API exactly as your own algorithm would.

First make sure the dependency resolves — see Installation. This example uses the gempba artifact, so no MPI runtime is needed.

docs.title: The shape of a GemPBA program
docs.text:
Every GemPBA program follows the same three beats:

  1. Set up a load balancer and a node manager, and configure the goal.
  2. Seed the recursion with a root node, then submit it.
  3. Wait for completion and read the result back.

Your algorithm is the recursive function in the middle. GemPBA owns the thread pool, the work queue, and the best-result bookkeeping.

docs.title: The recursive task
docs.text:
The task receives the worker thread id, your arguments, and the current Node. It does its per-node work, creates child nodes, and dispatches them back to the pool. Here the "work" is just a synthetic busy-wait; the leaf count is reported as the score.

import io.gempba.GemPBA;
import io.gempba.core.LoadBalancer;
import io.gempba.core.Node;
import io.gempba.core.NodeManager;
import io.gempba.value.Score;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

public class Benchmark {
    private final NodeManager nm;
    private final LoadBalancer lb;
    private final AtomicLong leafCount = new AtomicLong(0);

    public Benchmark(NodeManager nm, LoadBalancer lb) {
        this.nm = nm;
        this.lb = lb;
    }

    public void explore(long threadId, int depth, int maxDepth, Node parent) {
        if (depth == maxDepth) {                       // leaf: record a result
            int count = (int) leafCount.incrementAndGet();
            nm.tryUpdateResult(count, Score.make(count));
            return;
        }

        // A non-null parent threads provenance through the load balancer.
        Node vParent = (parent == null) ? GemPBA.createDummyNode(lb) : parent;

        Node left  = GemPBA.createExplicitNode(lb, vParent,
                (tid, node) -> explore(tid, depth + 1, maxDepth, node));
        Node right = GemPBA.createExplicitNode(lb, vParent,
                (tid, node) -> explore(tid, depth + 1, maxDepth, node));

        nm.tryLocalSubmit(left);   // hand one child to the pool
        nm.forward(right);         // recurse into the other on this thread
    }
}

The tryLocalSubmit / forward pair is the idiom: offer one branch to the thread pool, keep walking the other yourself. The quasi-horizontal load balancer decides which pending work is most valuable to hand out.

docs.title: The driver
docs.text:
import io.gempba.GemPBA;
import io.gempba.core.LoadBalancer;
import io.gempba.core.Node;
import io.gempba.core.NodeManager;
import io.gempba.task.Deserializer;
import io.gempba.task.Serializer;
import io.gempba.task.VoidNodeTask;
import io.gempba.value.BalancingPolicy;
import io.gempba.value.Goal;
import io.gempba.value.Score;
import io.gempba.value.ScoreType;

public class Main {
    private static final int MAX_DEPTH = 20;

    // The seed's Integer argument has to cross into native C++ code, so it is
    // converted to raw bytes on the way in and back to an int on the way out.
    // Child nodes never need this — see "How it works" for why.
    private static final Serializer<Integer> intToBytes =
            v -> new byte[]{(byte) (v >> 24), (byte) (v >> 16), (byte) (v >> 8), v.byteValue()};
    private static final Deserializer<Integer> bytesToInt =
            b -> ((b[0] & 0xFF) << 24) | ((b[1] & 0xFF) << 16) | ((b[2] & 0xFF) << 8) | (b[3] & 0xFF);

    static void main() throws InterruptedException {
        // 1. Set up
        LoadBalancer lb = GemPBA.createLoadBalancer(BalancingPolicy.QUASI_HORIZONTAL);
        NodeManager  nm = GemPBA.createNodeManager(lb);

        nm.setGoal(Goal.MAXIMISE, ScoreType.I32);   // maximise an int score
        nm.setThreadPoolSize(8);
        nm.setScore(Score.make(0));                  // initial score

        Benchmark benchmark = new Benchmark(nm, lb);

        // 2. Seed the recursion. The two translators above carry the seed's
        //    starting argument across the JNI boundary.
        Node seed = GemPBA.createSeedNode(lb,
                (VoidNodeTask<Integer>) (tid, depth, node) ->
                        benchmark.explore(tid, depth, MAX_DEPTH, node),
                0,             // initial argument: starting depth
                intToBytes,    // Integer -> byte[]  (crossing into C++)
                bytesToInt);   // byte[]  -> Integer (crossing back)

        double start = NodeManager.getWallTime();
        if (!nm.tryLocalSubmit(seed)) {
            throw new RuntimeException("unable to submit seed node");
        }

        // 3. Wait and read results
        nm.waitForCompletion();
        double elapsed = NodeManager.getWallTime() - start;

        System.out.printf("Score: %s%n", nm.getScore());
        System.out.printf("Elapsed: %.6f s%n", elapsed);
        nm.<Integer>getResult().ifPresent(r -> System.out.printf("Result: %d%n", r));

        GemPBA.shutdown();
    }
}

Why the intToBytes / bytesToInt translators?

They are the seed argument's passage into native code. Java cannot generate a typed native call the way C++ templates do, so GemPBA's Java binding moves a task's payload across the boundary as bytes. Only the seed needs them here — the child nodes capture their arguments straight from the Java closure. See How it works for the full story.

Java 25 entry point

The example uses the simpler entry point finalized in Java 25: static void main(), with no String[] args and no public. The binding targets JDK 25.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
mvn -pl mutithreading exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=io.gempba.mt.synthetic_void.Main

Or, in IntelliJ IDEA, open the project's pom.xml, let Maven resolve, and hit the green ▶ next to main.

To stop early, press Ctrl+C once: the run winds down gracefully and keeps the best result found so far. Stopping a Run covers the other ways to stop it and how a run says it ended.

docs.title: What changes for multiprocessing
docs.text:
Depend on gempba-mpi instead of gempba, and launch the program under mpiexec. The recursion keeps its shape, but work can now move to another process, so four things change:

  • A scheduler. Mpi.createScheduler(SchedulerTopology.SEMI_CENTRALIZED), from the io.gempba.mpi package, creates a Scheduler, which GemPBA.createLoadBalancer and GemPBA.createNodeManager take as their second argument.
  • Children carry bytes. A child that may go to another rank is created with a Serializer and a Deserializer, GemPBA.createExplicitNode(lb, parent, task, args, serializer, deserializer), and offered with nm.tryRemoteSubmit(node, runnableId) instead of tryLocalSubmit.
  • A runnable by id. GemPBA.runnableReturnNone(id, (threadId, bytes) -> …) tells every rank how to run a task that arrives as bytes.
  • One entry point on every rank. Rank 0 calls sched.run(nm, Map.of(id, runnable), seed, id) with the serialized seed, and every other rank calls sched.run(nm, Map.of(id, runnable)). It blocks until the whole run ends and returns how it ended.

See the multiprocessing module in gempba-java-examples for a full MPI program and its launcher.

docs.title: gempba
docs.text:
#include <gempba/gempba.hpp>

This is the facade for the entire library. It exposes the global accessors and every factory function, and it is the only header a multithreading program needs. An MPI program also includes <gempba/mpi.hpp> for its scheduler.

docs.title: Global accessors
docs.text:
These are how you reach the shared components from inside your algorithm, after they have been created in main().

load_balancer* lb = gempba::get_load_balancer();

Returns a pointer to the active load balancer.

node_manager& nm = gempba::get_node_manager();

Returns a reference to the node manager.

scheduler* s = gempba::get_scheduler();

Returns a pointer to the active scheduler. Throws when none has been created, as in a multithreading program.

scheduler* s = gempba::try_get_scheduler();

Non-throwing variant: returns nullptr when no scheduler has been created instead of throwing. Useful for read-only probes (telemetry uses it).

gempba::reset_node_manager();
gempba::reset_load_balancer();
gempba::reset_scheduler();

Destroy one component without shutting the rest down, so it can be created again: in tests, or between runs in one process. reset_node_manager() also gives back the signals create_node_manager took. shutdown() resets all three.

docs.title: Seed creation
docs.text:
auto seed = gempba::create_seed_node<void>(*lb, &my_func, std::make_tuple(initial_args...));

Creates the root of your search tree for a void function. Has no parent node.

auto seed = gempba::create_seed_node<MyReturnType>(*lb, &my_func, std::make_tuple(initial_args...));

Same for a non-void function.

auto dummy = gempba::create_dummy_node(*lb);

A placeholder parent with no function, for the seed's children: the seed runs with no parent, and children always need one.

docs.title: Load balancer and node manager
docs.text:
auto* lb = gempba::create_load_balancer(gempba::balancing_policy::QUASI_HORIZONTAL);

Create a load balancer using a built-in balancing policy. An MPI program passes its scheduler as well: gempba::create_load_balancer(policy, scheduler).

auto* lb = gempba::create_load_balancer(std::make_unique<MyLoadBalancer>());

Take ownership of a custom load balancer implementation. Your implementation holds the scheduler itself, if it uses one.

auto& nm = gempba::create_node_manager(lb);

Create the node manager. One per process. An MPI program passes its scheduler as well: gempba::create_node_manager(lb, scheduler).

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
auto child = gempba::create_explicit_node<void>(
    *lb, parent, &my_func, std::make_tuple(args...)
);

Create a child node inside your recursive function. Arguments are captured eagerly. Note the node factories take the load balancer by reference, while create_node_manager takes it as a pointer.

auto child = gempba::create_lazy_node<void>(
    *lb, parent, &my_func, args_initializer_fn
);

Lazy variant. Arguments are computed on demand, which is useful when preparing them is expensive and the branch might be pruned before it ever executes.

auto child = gempba::create_explicit_node<void>(
    *lb, parent, &my_func,
    std::make_tuple(args...),
    args_serializer_fn,    // Args... -> task_packet
    args_deserializer_fn   // task_packet -> tuple<Args...>
);

Create a child node with serializers. An MPI program needs them, because a node that runs on another rank sends its arguments there as bytes. create_lazy_node takes the same pair after its initializer.

auto child = gempba::create_from_bytes_node<void, Args...>(
    *lb, parent, &my_func, args_serializer_fn, args_deserializer_fn
);

A serializable child with no arguments yet: they arrive later as bytes, through the node's deserialize(task_packet).

The child factories throw if parent is null (gempba::check_not_null); a seed's children take a dummy node instead.

docs.title: The MPI component: <gempba/mpi.hpp>
docs.text:
#include <gempba/mpi.hpp>

The schedulers that spread a run across MPI ranks. They come with the MPI component, so a program that includes this header links gempba::mpi (see Installation). Every rank runs the same setup.

auto* s = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(gempba::mpi::scheduler_topology::SEMI_CENTRALIZED);

Create a scheduler using a built-in topology, and install telemetry over MPI. Every rank calls it.

auto* s = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(std::make_unique<MyScheduler>());

Install a custom scheduler, which runs on MPI, and telemetry over MPI. Every rank calls it.

auto* lb = gempba::create_load_balancer(gempba::balancing_policy::QUASI_HORIZONTAL, s);
auto& nm = gempba::create_node_manager(lb, s);

Pass the scheduler to the load balancer and the node manager.

s->run(nm, runnables, std::move(seed));

Run this rank's part of the search. Every rank calls it with the same runnables, and it returns once the whole run has ended. Only the root, rank 0, passes the seed. It returns how the run ended; see Stopping a run.

gempba::task_packet best = s->get_result();

The best result found across all ranks, once run has returned. Only the root may call it; any other rank throws.

auto visitor = gempba::mpi::get_default_mpi_stats_visitor();

Returns the bundled stats visitor for the MPI schedulers, ready to pass to the stats-collection API.

docs.title: Stopping a run
docs.text:
These come with <gempba/core/stop.hpp>, which this header includes. See Stopping a Run for how they fit together.

gempba::request_stop();

Ask the run to stop. Returns at once and is safe from any thread. Nodes that haven't started are pruned from then on, nodes already running finish, and the run returns its best result so far. Under MPI every rank stops. The first stop wins, by any trigger, until shutdown().

bool stopping = gempba::stop_requested();

Whether a stop was requested since the last shutdown(), by any trigger. Long work inside one node can poll it to return early.

gempba::stop_on_signals(false);

Whether SIGINT and SIGTERM stop the run gracefully instead of killing the process; on by default. While on, create_node_manager takes each of the two signals that nothing else handles yet, and shutdown() gives it back. A second SIGINT kills the process. Turning it off gives the signals back at once.

gempba::run_outcome outcome = scheduler->run(nm, runnables, std::move(seed));

How the run ended, the same on every rank: m_reason (end_reason::COMPLETED or INTERRUPTED), m_trigger (stop_trigger::NONE, CODE, SIGNAL or CONTROL) and m_signal, the signal's number for a stop by signal. MPI programs only.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
return gempba::shutdown();

Call at the end of main(). It destroys the scheduler, which finalizes MPI in an MPI program, so don't skip it there, and returns EXIT_SUCCESS. It also logs how a multithreading run ended, gives back the signals create_node_manager took, and clears the stop, so stop_requested() is false again.

docs.title: node_manager
docs.text:
node_manager is a concrete class. It is intentionally not extensible: every user of GemPBA interacts with the same control interface, and there is no reason for different implementations. You get it from gempba::get_node_manager() or from the factory function.

Think of it as your algorithm's control panel: configure the goal, submit work, wait for completion, and collect the result.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
nm.set_goal(gempba::goal::MAXIMISE, gempba::score_type::I32);
nm.set_goal(gempba::goal::MINIMISE, gempba::score_type::F64);

Set the optimization direction and the numeric type used to represent scores. Call before submitting any work. Available score types:

enum class score_type : std::uint8_t {
    I32, U_I32, I64, U_I64, F32, F64, F128
};

set_goal accepts I32, I64, F32, F64 and F128. U_I32 and U_I64 are in the enum, but set_goal has no starting score for them and throws.

I32 is the default. The score represents whatever "best" means for your problem: minimum cost, maximum coverage, shortest path length. You define the semantics. F128 maps to long double.

nm.set_score(gempba::score::make(0));

Set the initial best-known score. Your algorithm improves from this value.

nm.set_thread_pool_size(std::thread::hardware_concurrency());

Set the number of worker threads.

docs.title: Submitting work
docs.text:
bool queued = nm.try_local_submit(node);

Hand a node to a pool thread. Returns true when it was handed off or discarded, including earlier by the balancer; false when no thread was free and it ran on the calling thread instead.

nm.forward(node);

Execute the node on the current thread immediately. Even though this is a sequential call, wrapping the arguments in a node is not just boilerplate: the node stays registered in the exploration tree. If the library identifies an unresolved branch near the root of the current thread's subtree, a node still UNUSED, it can push that root-level node to an idle thread before the current thread gets back to it. By the time the current thread reaches that node, it is already flagged as consumed or discarded, and the entire branch is skipped. This is the mechanism that keeps threads from redundantly exploring subtrees that another thread has already claimed, and it is central to the quasi-horizontal load balancing strategy described in the paper and thesis.

nm.try_remote_submit(node, runnable_id);

Send a node to another rank, falling back to try_local_submit when no rank is free. Returns true when the node was sent or discarded, or had already been dispatched; false after the fallback. MPI programs only: it needs a scheduler.

nm.wait();

Block until all work is complete. Mainly to be used in the main thread after submitting the initial node(s). Worker threads should not call this, as they are expected to keep processing work until the entire tree is done.

The typical pattern inside a recursive function:

void my_func(std::thread::id tid, /* your args */, gempba::node parent) {
    // ... create left and right nodes ...

    nm.try_local_submit(left);  // offer to the thread pool
    nm.forward(right);          // run this one on the current thread
}

try_local_submit either sends left to an idle thread or runs it locally if no thread is free. forward always runs on the current thread. The load balancer makes the actual scheduling decision.

docs.title: Updating results
docs.text:
bool improved = nm.try_update_result(candidate, gempba::score::make(42));

Report a candidate solution found by your algorithm. Thread-safe. Compares the new score against the current best and updates only if the new one is better according to the goal you set. Returns true if the update happened.

nm.try_update_result(candidate, new_score, serializer);

MPI variant. Requires a serializer so the result can be transmitted across process boundaries:

std::function<task_packet(MyResult&)> serializer = [](MyResult& r) {
    return task_packet{/* r serialized */};
};

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text:
gempba::score best = nm.get_score();

Best score seen so far. Works in multithreading and MPI programs alike.

auto opt = nm.get_result<MyResult>();

Retrieve the result object stored by the first try_update_result overload, as a multithreading program does. Returns std::nullopt if no result has been set.

std::optional<result> raw = nm.get_result_bytes();

Retrieve the result stored as bytes by the serializer overload, as an MPI program does on each rank. Across ranks, read scheduler::get_result() on rank 0.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
double idle = nm.get_idle_time();

Seconds the pool threads spent idle waiting for work, per thread. High idle time usually means the tree is too narrow at the top, leaving threads with nothing to grab early on.

std::size_t reqs = nm.get_thread_request_count();

Number of times threads requested work from the load balancer.

int rank = nm.rank_me();

This process's rank. Returns -1 without a scheduler, as in a multithreading program.

double elapsed = node_manager::get_wall_time();

Wall-clock time in seconds since the epoch; subtract two readings for an elapsed time. Static method.

bool done = nm.is_done();

Whether the pool has no task left, queued or running, without blocking as wait() does.

std::future<std::any> f = nm.force_local_submit([] { return std::any{}; });

Queue a plain function on the pool, whether or not a thread is free, and get its future. It counts as a thread request.

gempba::balancing_policy policy = nm.get_balancing_policy();
unsigned int id = nm.generate_unique_id();

The load balancer's policy, and a fresh id from it. set_balancing_policy() only records a value on the node manager and doesn't change the balancer; pick the policy with create_load_balancer.

docs.title: node
docs.text:
#include <gempba/core/node.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

node is a final class. You cannot inherit from it. Internally it holds a shared_ptr<node_core> and delegates every operation to the underlying implementation through composition. This is what makes the framework pluggable: you can replace node_core with a custom implementation without changing anything in user code or in node itself.

Because node is just a shared pointer wrapper, copying it is cheap and safe. Two copies of the same node refer to the same underlying branch in the tree.

node satisfies node_traits<node>, which is the contract that load balancers and the scheduler depend on. See node_traits for the full interface.

docs.title: Factory functions
docs.text:
You do not construct nodes directly. Use the factory functions from gempba.hpp.

auto left = gempba::create_explicit_node<void>(
    *lb, parent, &my_func, std::make_tuple(args...)
);

Create a child node inside your recursive function. Arguments are captured eagerly.

auto child = gempba::create_lazy_node<void>(
    *lb, parent, &my_func, args_initializer_fn
);

Lazy variant. Arguments are computed on demand, useful when preparing them is expensive and the branch might be pruned before it executes.

auto seed = gempba::create_seed_node<void>(*lb, &my_func, std::make_tuple(initial_args...));

auto dummy = gempba::create_dummy_node(*lb);

Create a placeholder node. Used when you need a root context without arguments.

docs.title: Function signature requirements
docs.text:
Every function you parallelize must follow this pattern:

void my_func(std::thread::id tid, ArgType1 a, ArgType2 b, gempba::node parent);

For void functions. std::thread::id must be the first parameter and gempba::node must be the last. Your actual arguments go between them.

MyResult my_func(std::thread::id tid, ArgType1 a, ArgType2 b, gempba::node parent);

For non-void functions. Same signature rules apply.

The parent node represents the current call in the tree. You use it to create child nodes for the next level of recursion.

gempba::node copy = left;

if (left == right) { /* same underlying node_core */ }

Implements load_balancer. The primary scheduling strategy of GemPBA and the main algorithmic contribution of the original research. Designed for branching algorithms where subtree sizes are unknown and highly unbalanced, which is the common case.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text:
In a branch-and-bound search the recursion tree is highly unbalanced: one subtree might contain millions of nodes while its sibling contains three. Naive work-stealing picks whatever task is available, which is often a node near the leaves with almost no work left under it. Threads finish quickly and sit idle while one thread drowns in the large subtree.

Quasi-horizontal avoids this by handing out work near the root first. Nodes close to the root are the parents of the largest subtrees, so giving them to idle threads early gives each thread a roughly equal share of the work below.

docs.title: Per-thread root pointer
docs.text:
Each worker thread keeps a root pointer: the highest node in the tree that this thread still owns. When a thread hands a branch to another thread, the whole subtree under it goes along.

As branches finish or get handed out, the root pointer moves down. If the current root has only one child left, there's nothing to share at that level, so the pointer moves to that child. It keeps going until it reaches a node with two or more children, a leaf, or the parent of the node being submitted. This is the root correction step.

docs.title: Node states
docs.text:
Every node starts out UNUSED. Once the calling thread starts its runnable, the node is RUNNING, and when the runnable returns it becomes FORWARDED. A node handed to a pool thread becomes PUSHED, one sent to another process becomes SENT_TO_ANOTHER_PROCESS, and one whose lazy arguments say it isn't worth exploring becomes DISCARDED.

At any moment, a thread's RUNNING nodes form a single path, from the thread's root down to the node whose runnable is executing right now. Only the last node on that path is actually executing. The ones above it are waiting for their children to return. Every other node in the tree hangs off this path and is either waiting or already done.

docs.title: Submission algorithm
docs.text:
When you call try_local_submit, the balancer:

  1. Returns true right away if the node was already handed out (PUSHED, SENT_TO_ANOTHER_PROCESS or DISCARDED), no matter who handed it out.
  2. Returns false if the pool is full or another thread is using the balancer. The node then runs in the calling thread, just like with forward.
  3. Hands out the root's waiting children first. As long as the thread's root has an UNUSED child, it gives the leftmost one to an idle thread and corrects the root. It never hands out a RUNNING child, wherever that child sits.
  4. Prunes the submitted node and corrects the root past any single-child nodes this leaves behind.
  5. Gives the node to a thread if should_branch() is true. Otherwise it marks the node DISCARDED.

forward runs the node in the calling thread if it's still UNUSED, then prunes it and corrects the root.

You can forward and submit siblings in any order. If the balancer already handed a sibling out, forward skips it and try_local_submit just returns true. This also means a node you create under a parent can be handed out even if your code never forwards or submits it.

Tree navigation calls used:

p_node.get_root()                   // current root for this thread
p_root.get_children_count()         // branches remaining at root level
p_root.get_leftmost_child()         // first root-level child, then...
p_child.get_right_sibling()         // ...its siblings, left to right
p_child.get_state()                 // only UNUSED children are handed out

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: This is the default and recommended strategy for all branching algorithms. Use Work-Stealing only when you need a baseline for benchmarking.

docs.title: Work-Stealing
docs.text:
auto* lb = gempba::create_load_balancer(gempba::balancing_policy::WORK_STEALING);

Implements load_balancer. A deliberately simple strategy: tasks are pushed to the thread pool queue as they arrive, idle threads pick them up in order. No tree structure is inspected, no root pointer is maintained.

docs.title: Submission algorithm
docs.text:
When try_local_submit is called:

  1. Attempts a non-blocking lock on the internal mutex.
  2. Returns false immediately if the lock is unavailable or the pool is full.
  3. Prunes the node and delegates it to a thread if should_branch() is true.

No root tracking. No sibling search. No root correction.
