docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
Primarily as a comparison baseline — for reproducing the benchmarks from the original paper, or for sanity-checking whether the overhead of Quasi-Horizontal is a net negative on a specific workload.

On uniformly balanced trees, work-stealing may perform comparably to quasi-horizontal. On the unbalanced trees characteristic of real branch-and-bound problems it loses ground: stolen tasks tend to be near the leaves, carrying little remaining work, so threads finish quickly and idle.

docs.title: MPI Centralized
docs.text:
#include <gempba/mpi.hpp>

auto* s = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(gempba::mpi::scheduler_topology::CENTRALIZED);

Implements scheduler. An actively routing MPI scheduler. Uses MPI as the IPC transport: Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI, whichever your build compiles gempba::mpi against.

The coordinator (rank 0) is an active participant: workers send excess tasks to the coordinator, and the coordinator dispatches them to available workers. Every task handoff traverses the coordinator twice — once inbound, once outbound. At small process counts this is negligible; at scale the coordinator becomes a bottleneck.

For the full protocol walkthrough and comparison with the semi-centralized topology, see Scheduler Topologies.

docs.title: Inside the scheduler
docs.text:
Inside the centralized scheduler: rank 0's coordinator loop keeps a bounded priority queue of tasks, the process states, the global best score and the root of termination detection; four duplicated communicators carry tasks and states, fullness signals, scores and telemetry; on every worker, pool threads put one spare task in the outgoing slot while rank 0 isn't full, and the MPI thread sends it to rank 0 Rank 0 Communicators Every worker rank Coordinator loop the thread that called run Task queue by priority · 1000 × ranks or 10 GB Process states AVAILABLE · RUNNING Global best score broadcast when it improves Termination detector the root: a deficit, no parent dispatches queued tasks to available workers; runs none itself Pool threads run nodes; the load balancer offers a spare node to try_open_transmission_channel Outgoing slot: one task while rank 0 isn't full MPI thread the thread that called run; every MPI call goes through it. It probes the communicators, runs received tasks on the pool, sends the slot to rank 0, proposes scores, acknowledges tasks and reports its state world TASK_FOR_CENTER · TASK_FROM_CENTER RUNNING / AVAILABLE_STATE TASK_RECEIVED · STOP · TERMINATION center fullness CENTER_IS_FULL · CENTER_IS_FREE global score SCORE_PROPOSAL → rank 0 SCORE_UPDATE → every worker telemetry rank and node frames → rank 0 each an MPI_Comm_dup of MPI_COMM_WORLD, so gempba's messages never meet yours Every task goes through rank 0's queue: workers send their spare tasks there and take new ones from it; no task goes from worker to worker.
  • Rank 0 runs the coordinator loop on the thread that called scheduler::run. It keeps every spare task in a priority queue and hands them out to available workers; past its limits it tells the workers to keep their tasks.
  • Every worker works as in the semi-centralized scheduler: pool threads run nodes and, while rank 0 isn't full, put a spare task in the one-task outgoing slot; the MPI thread makes every MPI call and sends that slot to rank 0.
  • Four communicators, each an MPI_Comm_dup of MPI_COMM_WORLD: tasks, states, acknowledgements and termination on one, the full and free signals on another, scores on a third, and telemetry on its own.

docs.title: Coordinator responsibilities
docs.text:
• Maintain a bounded task queue
  • Maintain the process status table (RUNNING, AVAILABLE)
  • Dispatch queued tasks to available workers
  • Broadcast the global best value

The coordinator's queue is bounded by compile-time limits: 1000 tasks per process, times the number of ranks, or 10 GB of memory. Past either one it broadcasts CENTER_IS_FULL, and workers run their tasks locally instead of sending them. Once the queue is below 80% of the task limit and memory below 90%, it broadcasts CENTER_IS_FREE and workers send again. It never rejects a task it has received.

docs.title: Worker responsibilities
docs.text:
• Explore the search tree via the thread pool
  • Send excess tasks to the coordinator when it is not full
  • Accept tasks dispatched by the coordinator
  • Update the local best value when the coordinator broadcasts a new global best

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Benchmarking and comparison only. The centralized topology exists to reproduce the experimental results from the original paper. For production use, prefer MPI Semi-Centralized.

docs.title: MPI Semi-Centralized
docs.text:
#include <gempba/mpi.hpp>

auto* s = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(gempba::mpi::scheduler_topology::SEMI_CENTRALIZED);

Implements scheduler. The recommended MPI scheduler. Uses MPI as the IPC transport: Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI, whichever your build compiles gempba::mpi against.

The coordinator (rank 0) maintains a lightweight state table — process statuses, process assignments, global best value — and pushes assignment signals proactively. It never holds or routes tasks. Workers exchange tasks directly with each other, point-to-point, after the coordinator has confirmed the destination is idle. This eliminates the bounce-back problem without making the coordinator a bottleneck.

For the full protocol walkthrough, message sequence diagrams, and comparison with the centralized topology, see Scheduler Topologies.

docs.title: Inside the scheduler
docs.text:
Inside the semi-centralized scheduler: rank 0's coordinator loop keeps process states, waiting processes, the global best score and the root of termination detection; four duplicated communicators carry tasks and states, assignments, scores and telemetry; on every worker, pool threads put one spare task in the outgoing slot, and the MPI thread sends it straight to the worker's waiting process Rank 0 Communicators Every worker rank Coordinator loop the thread that called run Process states AVAILABLE · RUNNING · ASSIGNED Waiting processes who sends to whom next Global best score broadcast when it improves Termination detector the root: a deficit, no parent no thread pool and no tasks: it runs no search itself Pool threads run nodes; the load balancer offers a spare node to try_open_transmission_channel Outgoing slot: one task while a process waits for it MPI thread the thread that called run; every MPI call goes through it. It probes the communicators, runs received tasks on the pool, sends the slot to the process waiting for it, proposes scores, acknowledges tasks and reports its state world TASK · RUNNING_STATE AVAILABLE_STATE · TASK_RECEIVED STOP · TERMINATION · results next process NEXT_PROCESS: an assignment global score SCORE_PROPOSAL → rank 0 SCORE_UPDATE → every worker telemetry rank and node frames → rank 0 each an MPI_Comm_dup of MPI_COMM_WORLD, so gempba's messages never meet yours its waiting process, another worker rank TASK, straight to the waiting process, on the world communicator The coordinator never holds or forwards a task: it only says who should send to whom.
  • Rank 0 runs the coordinator loop on the thread that called scheduler::run. It holds the state table and the root of termination detection, and runs no search itself.
  • Every worker splits the job between two kinds of thread. Pool threads run nodes; when the load balancer finds a spare node and the rank has a process waiting for work, try_open_transmission_channel succeeds and force_push puts the serialized task in a one-task outgoing slot. The MPI thread, the one that called scheduler::run, makes every MPI call: it probes the communicators in turn, runs each task it receives on the pool, sends the slot straight to the waiting process, proposes better scores, and acknowledges tasks.
  • Four communicators, each an MPI_Comm_dup of MPI_COMM_WORLD, keep the traffic apart: tasks, states, acknowledgements and termination on one, assignments on another, scores on a third, and telemetry on its own.

docs.title: Coordinator responsibilities
docs.text:
• Maintain the authoritative process status table (AVAILABLE, RUNNING, ASSIGNED)
  • Maintain the process assignment table (which idle process is waiting on which busy one)
  • Maintain the global best value and broadcast updates to all workers
  • Before the seed, send every worker its initial assignment: a binomial tree over ranks 1 to N-1, or the tree given to set_custom_initial_topology
  • Seed the initial task to the first worker

The coordinator never holds a task queue. Its memory usage is independent of the number of pending tasks.

docs.title: Worker responsibilities
docs.text:
• Explore the search tree via the thread pool
  • Notify the coordinator on state transitions (RUNNING_STATE, AVAILABLE_STATE)
  • Send the highest-priority pending task directly to the assigned waiting process
  • Update the local best value when the coordinator broadcasts a new global best

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Production. The semi-centralized scheduler is always at least as fast as the centralized one and scales better as the number of processes grows. Use MPI Centralized only for reproducing paper benchmarks.

docs.title: Default MPI stats
docs.text:
// src/mpi/private/impl/schedulers/default_mpi_stats.hpp: private to the MPI component

The built-in stats implementation for the MPI schedulers. Programs read it through default_mpi_stats_visitor or the visit lambda below, not by including it. Every rank owns one during a run, rank 0 included. After synchronize_stats(), which every rank calls, rank 0 holds one instance per rank.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
visit hands over each value under these keys:

Key Type Meaning rank int The rank these stats belong to. received_task_count std::size_t Tasks this rank received from other ranks. sent_task_count std::size_t Tasks this rank sent to other ranks. total_thread_requests std::size_t Times this rank's pool threads asked the load balancer for work. idle_time double Seconds this rank's pool threads spent idle, per thread (node_manager::get_idle_time()). elapsed_time double Seconds from the start of this rank's run to its end (MPI_Wtime). coordinator_messages_handled std::size_t On the coordinator, rank 0: running and available reports, tasks in and out, score proposals and score broadcasts it handled. 0 on workers.

Rank 0's entry is never empty: it holds the coordinator's own counts and elapsed time.

docs.title: Reading the stats
docs.text:
Use default_mpi_stats_visitor to extract these fields after the run:

scheduler->synchronize_stats();   // collective: every rank calls it

if (scheduler->is_root()) {
    auto stats_vec = scheduler->get_stats_vector();   // one entry per rank, rank 0 first

    for (std::size_t rank = 0; rank < stats_vec.size(); ++rank) {
        gempba::default_mpi_stats_visitor v;
        stats_vec[rank]->visit(&v);

        std::cout << "Rank " << rank << "\n"
                  << "  received:  " << v.m_received_task_count << "\n"
                  << "  sent:      " << v.m_sent_task_count     << "\n"
                  << "  idle time: " << v.m_idle_time           << " s per thread\n"
                  << "  elapsed:   " << v.m_elapsed_time        << " s\n";
    }
}

Alternatively, use the lambda overload to read values by key without a visitor:

stats_vec[rank]->visit([](const std::string& key, std::any&& value) {
    if (key == "elapsed_time") {
        std::cout << "elapsed: " << std::any_cast<double>(value) << " s\n";
    }
});

docs.title: default_mpi_stats_visitor
docs.text:
#include <gempba/mpi/default_mpi_stats_visitor.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba/mpi.hpp

The built-in stats_visitor for the MPI scheduler stats. After calling visit, all fields are populated as plain public members. It reads the keys listed under Default MPI stats, except rank.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
std::size_t m_received_task_count;

Tasks the rank received from other ranks.

std::size_t m_sent_task_count;

Tasks the rank sent to other ranks.

std::size_t m_total_thread_requests;

Times the rank's pool threads asked the load balancer for work.

double m_idle_time;

Seconds the rank's pool threads spent idle, per thread.

double m_elapsed_time;

Seconds from the start of the rank's run to its end.

std::size_t m_coordinator_messages_handled;

On the coordinator, rank 0: running and available reports, tasks in and out, score proposals and score broadcasts it handled. 0 on workers.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
// After scheduler->run(...) returns, on every rank:
scheduler->synchronize_stats();   // collective

if (scheduler->is_root()) {
    auto stats_vec = scheduler->get_stats_vector();   // one entry per rank, rank 0 (the coordinator) first

    for (std::size_t rank = 0; rank < stats_vec.size(); ++rank) {
        gempba::default_mpi_stats_visitor v;
        stats_vec[rank]->visit(&v);

        std::cout << "Rank " << rank << ":\n"
                  << "  received:  " << v.m_received_task_count << "\n"
                  << "  sent:      " << v.m_sent_task_count     << "\n"
                  << "  idle time: " << v.m_idle_time           << " s per thread\n"
                  << "  elapsed:   " << v.m_elapsed_time        << " s\n";
    }
}

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
These are the pluggable contracts of GemPBA. Each one defines what an implementation must do without prescribing how. You interact with them if you are replacing a built-in component with a custom one — a GPU-backed node, a domain-specific scheduling strategy.

Interface Purpose node_core The abstract node — owns an instance, tracks tree position, manages lifecycle node_traits The full interface contract every node must satisfy load_balancer Thread-level work distribution within a process scheduler Process-level coordination over MPI — every rank calls its run serial_runnable Type erasure for functions that cross process boundaries stats Runtime metrics collection stats_visitor Format-agnostic readout of collected metrics

docs.title: load_balancer
docs.text:
#include <gempba/core/load_balancer.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

Abstract interface for thread-level work distribution within a single process. node_manager holds a pointer to one and routes all submission calls through it.

Built-in implementations: Quasi-Horizontal (recommended), Work-Stealing (baseline).

docs.text:
enum balancing_policy { QUASI_HORIZONTAL, WORK_STEALING };   // gempba::balancing_policy, <gempba/utils/gempba_utils.hpp>
The built-in strategies, at namespace scope. Returned by get_balancing_policy() and passed to create_load_balancer.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
virtual void set_thread_pool_size(unsigned int size) = 0;
Set number of worker threads. Call before submitting any work.

docs.title: Task submission
docs.text:
virtual bool try_local_submit(node& p_node) = 0;
Hand p_node to an idle pool thread. Returns true when it was handed off or discarded, or a balancer had already dispatched it; false when no thread was free, in which case the balancer has already run it on the calling thread.

virtual void forward(node& p_node) = 0;
Execute p_node on the calling thread immediately.

virtual bool try_remote_submit(node& p_node, int runnable_id) = 0;
Send p_node to another process through the scheduler, falling back to try_local_submit when no process is free. runnable_id selects the matching serial_runnable on the remote side. Returns true when it was sent, discarded or already dispatched; false after the fallback. Throws without a scheduler, so it belongs to MPI programs.

virtual std::future<std::any> force_local_submit(std::function<std::any()>&&) = 0;
Submit an arbitrary callable to the thread pool and return a future. Internal use only.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
[[nodiscard]] virtual double       get_idle_time()            const = 0;
[[nodiscard]] virtual bool         is_done()                  const = 0;
[[nodiscard]] virtual std::size_t  get_thread_request_count() const = 0;
[[nodiscard]] virtual unsigned int get_thread_pool_size()     const = 0;
[[nodiscard]] virtual std::size_t  get_tasks_running_count()  const = 0;

get_idle_time(): cumulative wall-clock seconds the pool spent waiting for work, averaged per thread. get_starved_idle_time() / get_imbalanced_idle_time(): the part of that idle time spent while no task ran in the pool, and while other threads ran tasks; 0 for a balancer that doesn't split it. get_spawn_rejected_pool_full_count() / get_spawn_remote_rejected_count(): submissions that found the pool full, and remote submissions that found no process free. is_done(): true when queue is empty and all threads are idle. get_thread_request_count(): total tasks submitted since startup. get_thread_pool_size(): current worker-thread count in the pool. get_tasks_running_count(): tasks executing on the pool right now. Together with get_thread_pool_size() this is what telemetry samples for the live rank frames.

docs.title: node_core
docs.text:
#include <gempba/core/node_core.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

Abstract base class for node implementations. Extends node_traits<shared_ptr<node_core>> — the implementation-layer handle type is a shared pointer. The default concrete class is node_core_impl in detail/nodes/node_core_impl.hpp.

node (the public handle) wraps a shared_ptr<node_core> and delegates every operation through it. Swapping the underlying node_core subclass changes behavior without touching user code.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text: Implement every pure virtual method from node_traits with T = shared_ptr<node_core>. No additional methods are declared beyond that contract.

docs.title: Custom implementation
docs.text:
class MyNodeCore : public gempba::node_core {
    // implement all node_traits<shared_ptr<node_core>> pure virtuals
};

auto my_node = gempba::create_custom_node(std::make_unique<MyNodeCore>());

Warning

Study node_core_impl before writing from scratch — pay attention to should_branch() (lazy argument initialization), prune() (child list cleanup), and the root-pointer semantics used by the quasi-horizontal load balancer.

Realistic reasons to subclass: GPU execution in run(), custom allocators, domain-specific serialization.

docs.title: scheduler
docs.text:
#include <gempba/core/scheduler.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

Abstract interface for process-level coordination. Every rank holds one scheduler and calls its run; rank 0, the root, seeds the run and reads its results. Extends scheduler_traits.

Built-in implementations use MPI (Open MPI, MPICH or MS-MPI, whichever your build compiles against) and come with the MPI component, gempba::mpi. A custom scheduler is installed with gempba::mpi::create_scheduler, which also sets up telemetry over MPI, so it runs on MPI too. For protocol details see Scheduler Topologies.

docs.title: Factory
docs.text:
#include <gempba/mpi.hpp>

auto* s = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(gempba::mpi::scheduler_topology::SEMI_CENTRALIZED);
auto* s = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(std::make_unique<MyScheduler>());
scheduler_topology Description SEMI_CENTRALIZED The coordinator assigns workers; tasks travel point-to-point. Recommended. CENTRALIZED All tasks route through the coordinator. Benchmarking only.

docs.title: scheduler_traits (shared base)
docs.text:
The base of scheduler.

virtual void barrier() = 0;
Global synchronization point — blocks until all processes reach this call.

[[nodiscard]] virtual int rank_me()    const = 0;
[[nodiscard]] virtual int world_size() const = 0;
Process identity within the communicator. Rank 0 is the root; in the built-in schedulers it is also the coordinator.

[[nodiscard]] virtual std::unique_ptr<stats> get_stats() const = 0;
This process's runtime metrics. Workers hold compute stats; the coordinator holds its own counts and elapsed time.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
virtual void set_goal(goal, score_type) = 0;
Set optimization direction (MAXIMISE/MINIMISE) and score numeric type. Must match the goal set on node_manager.

virtual void set_custom_initial_topology(tree&&) = 0;
Replace the default startup waiting list, a binomial tree over the workers, with a custom process assignment tree. The semi-centralized scheduler uses it; the centralized one, where every task goes through the coordinator, ignores it.

docs.title: Running a search
docs.text:
run_outcome run(node_manager& nm,
                std::map<int, std::shared_ptr<serial_runnable>> runnables,
                std::optional<task_bundle> seed = std::nullopt);
Run this rank's part of the search. Every rank calls it with the same runnables, and it returns once the whole run has ended, with how it ended, the same on every rank; the root also logs it (see Stopping a Run). Only the root passes the seed; a root without one, or another rank with one, throws std::invalid_argument. Incoming task_packets are dispatched to the matching serial_runnable by ID.

[[nodiscard]] task_packet         get_result();
[[nodiscard]] std::vector<result> get_all_results();
get_result() — single best result found across all ranks. get_all_results() — each rank's best result, indexed by rank and empty where a rank found none. Both are for the root once run has returned; any other rank throws std::logic_error.

[[nodiscard]] bool is_root() const;
Whether this rank is the root, rank 0.

docs.title: Task transfer
docs.text:
virtual unsigned int force_push(task_packet&& task, int function_id) = 0;
Hand task to another rank, to run under the runnable function_id. Returns the receiving rank.

virtual std::optional<transmission_guard> try_open_transmission_channel() = 0;
Non-blocking lock on the outgoing transmission mutex. Returns nullopt if the channel is already in use, and in the built-in schedulers also when there is nowhere to send: the semi-centralized one has no waiting process assigned to this rank, or the centralized coordinator is full.

docs.title: Stats collection
docs.text:
virtual void synchronize_stats() = 0;
Gather every rank's stats on rank 0. Collective: every rank calls it after run() returns.

[[nodiscard]] virtual std::vector<std::unique_ptr<stats>> get_stats_vector() const = 0;
One stats entry per rank, index 0 included: the coordinator's own counts and elapsed time. Call only on rank 0 after synchronize_stats().

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
[[nodiscard]] virtual double elapsed_time() const = 0;
Wall-clock seconds from run start to termination.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
[[nodiscard]] virtual std::size_t get_pending_request_count() const = 0;
Outstanding requests in the scheduler queue: the centralized coordinator's queued tasks, and always 0 for the semi-centralized scheduler, which queues none. Sampled by telemetry for the rank frames.

[[nodiscard]] virtual std::string_view get_name() const;   // "custom" unless overridden
The name telemetry reports for this scheduler: "semi_centralized" or "centralized" for the built-ins.

[[nodiscard]] virtual rank_role role_of(int rank) const;   // rank_role::WORKER unless overridden
The role a rank plays: rank_role::COORDINATOR, which coordinates and runs no tasks, or rank_role::WORKER, which runs tasks (<gempba/core/rank_role.hpp>). The built-ins answer COORDINATOR for rank 0. Each rank reports its own role to telemetry once, at startup, so the answer must stay fixed for the whole run.

docs.title: Custom implementation
docs.text:
class MyScheduler : public gempba::scheduler {
    // implement the remaining scheduler and scheduler_traits pure virtuals
protected:
    gempba::run_outcome do_run(gempba::node_manager& nm,
                               std::map<int, std::shared_ptr<gempba::serial_runnable>> runnables,
                               std::optional<gempba::task_bundle> seed) override;
    gempba::task_packet do_get_result() override;
    std::vector<gempba::result> do_get_all_results() override;
};

auto* s = gempba::mpi::create_scheduler(std::make_unique<MyScheduler>());

run, get_result and get_all_results check the caller's rank, then call these. do_run is this rank's part of the run, with seed set exactly on the root, and returns the same run_outcome on every rank. gempba's custom-schedulers.md lists what a custom scheduler must do to feed telemetry and to take part in a stop.

docs.title: serial_runnable
docs.text:
#include <gempba/core/serial_runnable.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

Type erasure for functions that cross process boundaries. Each serial_runnable wraps one typed function and exposes a uniform interface to the scheduler — bytes in, bytes out, routed by integer ID. The scheduler never touches function types.

docs.title: Member functions
docs.text:
virtual int get_id() const = 0;
Unique integer identifying this function across all processes.

virtual std::optional<std::shared_future<task_packet>>
operator()(node_manager& nm, const task_packet& task) = 0;
Deserialize arguments from task, call the wrapped function, return serialized result — or std::nullopt for void functions.

docs.title: Void function
docs.text:
auto runnable = gempba::runnables::return_none::create<Arg1, Arg2, ...>(
    FUNCTION_ID,
    &my_func,
    deserializer   // std::function<std::tuple<Arg1, Arg2, ...>(const task_packet&&)>
);

docs.title: Non-void function
docs.text:
auto runnable = gempba::runnables::return_value::create<ReturnType, Arg1, Arg2, ...>(
    FUNCTION_ID,
    &my_func,
    deserializer,  // std::function<std::tuple<Arg1, Arg2, ...>(const task_packet&&)>
    serializer     // std::function<task_packet(ReturnType)>
);

docs.title: Registering runnables
docs.text:
std::map<int, std::shared_ptr<gempba::serial_runnable>> runnables;
runnables[FUNCTION_ID]       = runnable_a;
runnables[OTHER_FUNCTION_ID] = runnable_b;

std::optional<gempba::task_bundle> seed;      // set on the root only
s->run(nm, runnables, std::move(seed));      // every rank; blocks until the whole run has ended

When a task_packet arrives tagged with FUNCTION_ID, the scheduler calls operator() on the matching runnable. All template machinery (deserialization, dispatch, serialization) stays inside detail/runnables/ — nothing typed crosses a process boundary.

docs.title: stats_visitor
docs.text:
#include <gempba/stats/stats_visitor.hpp>  // gempba.hpp only declares it; <gempba/mpi.hpp> includes it

Abstract interface for reading out metrics from a stats object. Decouples collection (what is measured) from presentation (how it is reported).

docs.title: Member functions
docs.text:
virtual void visit(const stats&) = 0;
Called by stats::visit(stats_visitor*). Map field names from the stats object to member variables or output targets of your choosing.

docs.title: Custom implementation
docs.text:
class MyStatsVisitor : public gempba::stats_visitor {
public:
    std::size_t task_count{};
    double      idle_seconds{};

    void visit(const gempba::stats& s) override {
        s.visit([this](const std::string& key, std::any&& value) {
            if (key == "received_task_count")
                task_count = std::any_cast<std::size_t>(value);
            else if (key == "idle_time")
                idle_seconds = std::any_cast<double>(value);
        });
    }
};

MyStatsVisitor v;
stats_ptr->visit(&v);

Available field names depend on the concrete stats implementation. For the built-in MPI stats, see default_mpi_stats_visitor.

docs.title: stats
docs.text:
#include <gempba/stats/stats.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

Abstract interface for a single process's runtime metrics. The scheduler owns one instance per process and returns it after the run. Not constructed directly.

docs.title: Member functions
docs.text:
[[nodiscard]] virtual task_packet serialize() const = 0;
Serialize metrics to bytes for inter-process transfer. Called internally by synchronize_stats().

[[nodiscard]] virtual std::vector<std::string> labels() const = 0;
Names of all tracked fields in declaration order.

virtual void visit(std::function<void(const std::string&, std::any&&)>) const = 0;
Call visitor once per field with field name and value as std::any. Use std::any_cast<T> to retrieve typed values.

virtual void visit(stats_visitor*) const = 0;
Dispatch to a typed stats_visitor.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
// Lambda visitor
stats_ptr->visit([](const std::string& key, std::any&& value) {
    if (key == "idle_time")
        std::cout << std::any_cast<double>(value) << " s per thread\n";
    if (key == "received_task_count")
        std::cout << std::any_cast<std::size_t>(value) << "\n";
});

// Typed visitor
MyStatsVisitor v;
stats_ptr->visit(&v);

docs.title: Custom implementation
docs.text:
class MyStats : public gempba::stats {
public:
    std::size_t my_counter{};
    double      my_duration{};

    task_packet serialize() const override { /* encode fields */ }

    std::vector<std::string> labels() const override {
        return {"my_counter", "my_duration"};
    }

    void visit(std::function<void(const std::string&, std::any&&)> v) const override {
        v("my_counter", my_counter);
        v("my_duration", my_duration);
    }

    void visit(gempba::stats_visitor* v) const override { v->visit(*this); }
};

Key names passed to the lambda visitor must be stable — stats_visitor implementations identify fields by those strings.

docs.title: queue
docs.text:
#include <gempba/utils/queue.hpp>  // not included by gempba.hpp

queue<T> is a thread-safe FIFO queue. It wraps std::queue<T> with a std::mutex, making push, pop, and empty-check safe to call from multiple threads concurrently without external synchronization.

Sourced from CTPL by Vitaliy Vitsentiy (Apache 2.0).

Used internally by the MPI schedulers for their outgoing tasks. Not intended for direct use in user code.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
bool push(const T& value);

Adds value to the back of the queue. Always succeeds; returns true.

bool pop(T& out);

Removes the front element into out. Returns false if the queue is empty, leaving out unchanged.

bool empty();

Returns true if the queue contains no elements.

All three methods lock the internal mutex for their duration.

docs.title: result
docs.text:
#include <gempba/utils/result.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

result pairs a score with a task_packet. It represents a candidate solution found during the search: the quality of the solution and its serialized form ready for retrieval or transmission.

node_manager stores the best result seen so far and returns it after the run completes. In multiprocessing mode, the worker that found the best solution reports it to the coordinator as a result; the coordinator selects the overall best when collecting final answers.

Convenience wrapper around score::get_loose<int>(). Useful for quick comparisons when the score type is known to be integral.

docs.title: score
docs.text:
#include <gempba/utils/score.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

score is a fixed-size, type-erased numeric value. It holds exactly one value of a supported numeric type in a 16-byte payload plus a 1-byte type tag, making it trivially copyable and safe for IPC transmission without serialization overhead.

It is the currency of the optimization objective: every call to nm.set_score(), nm.try_update_result(), and nm.get_score() works in terms of score.

static_assert(sizeof(score) == 17);               // 1 byte tag + 16 byte payload
static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<score>);
static_assert(std::is_standard_layout_v<score>);

docs.title: score_type
docs.text:
enum class score_type : std::uint8_t {
    I32, U_I32, I64, U_I64, F32, F64, F128
};

Identifies which numeric type a score holds. F128 maps to long double.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
template<typename T>
static constexpr score score::make(T value) noexcept;

Factory for all supported types. The template parameter is deduced — pass the value directly:

auto s = gempba::score::make(42);      // score_type::I32
auto s = gempba::score::make(42u);     // score_type::U_I32
auto s = gempba::score::make(42LL);    // score_type::I64
auto s = gempba::score::make(3.14f);   // score_type::F32
auto s = gempba::score::make(3.14);    // score_type::F64
auto s = gempba::score::make(3.14L);   // score_type::F128

docs.title: Accessors
docs.text:
template<typename T>
[[nodiscard]] T get() const;

Returns the stored value as T. Throws std::runtime_error if T does not match the stored type exactly.

template<typename T>
[[nodiscard]] bool try_get(T& out) const noexcept;

Non-throwing variant. Returns false and leaves out unchanged if the type does not match.

template<typename T>
[[nodiscard]] T get_loose() const noexcept;

Returns the stored value converted to T regardless of the stored type, using static_cast. Use when you need the value as a specific type for display or comparison and do not care about the original type.

[[nodiscard]] std::string to_string() const noexcept;

task_bundle pairs a task_packet with a runnable_id. It is the unit of inter-process task transfer: when a worker sends work to another process, it wraps the serialized arguments in a task_bundle so the receiving end knows which serial_runnable to dispatch it to.

In an MPI program, rank 0 builds one for the seed it passes to scheduler::run: std::optional<gempba::task_bundle> seed; if (scheduler->is_root()) { seed.emplace(packet, runnable_id); }. Otherwise node factory functions and the scheduler produce and consume them internally.

docs.title: task_packet
docs.text:
#include <gempba/utils/task_packet.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

task_packet is a raw byte buffer — a std::vector<std::byte> with a richer construction interface. It is the wire format for everything that crosses a process boundary in GemPBA: serialized function arguments, serialized return values, and serialized results.

Your serializer lambdas produce task_packet values; your deserializer lambdas consume them:

// Serializer: Args... → task_packet
auto serializer = [](const MyGraph& g, int depth) -> gempba::task_packet {
    std::vector<std::byte> buf = /* encode g and depth */;
    return gempba::task_packet{std::move(buf)};
};

// Deserializer: task_packet → tuple<Args...>
auto deserializer = [](const gempba::task_packet& p) {
    return std::make_tuple(/* decode graph */, /* decode depth */);
};

#include <gempba/utils/transmission_guard.hpp>  // included automatically via gempba.hpp

transmission_guard is a RAII wrapper around a std::unique_lock<std::mutex>. It holds a mutex lock for exactly the duration of an IPC send, releasing it automatically on destruction.

Non-copyable. Movable.

Returned by scheduler::try_open_transmission_channel() and held by the load balancers while they send a task to another rank. Not intended for direct use in user code.

Used internally by the semi-centralized scheduler to represent the process assignment topology built during the startup phase. Not intended for direct use in user code.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
GemPBA ships with a built-in runtime telemetry system. While your search runs, every rank publishes a live stream of what it is doing: tasks started, sent, received, and running; where its thread-pool idle time went; scheduler backlog and timing; per-process CPU and memory; and a rank-to-rank traffic list, alongside per-host CPU and memory and the full hardware topology. It is on by default, with or without the MPI component, so your production runs are observable out of the box with nothing to wire up.

Built in, on by default

Telemetry is compiled into the library, so there is no build flag to enable it; it starts automatically when the runtime comes up. Opt out at runtime with gempba::telemetry::disable() (see Configuration). Hardware-topology fields are populated when GemPBA is built with hwloc (GEMPBA_HWLOC, on for releases); without it, core/socket counts read as 0 and everything else still works.

docs.title: Why it's in the box
docs.text: Live, per-rank observability across a distributed run is normally a project of its own: a metrics sidecar to deploy, a transport that won't perturb the workload, a schema everyone has to agree on, and some way to reach processes scattered across nodes. GemPBA handles that part. Telemetry rides its own private MPI communicator (MPI_Comm_dup), so it never collides with application traffic; it aggregates every rank into a single stream; and it exposes that stream on a channel a client can not only read but steer. Emission cadence is retunable live, mid-run, without restarting the job (see Configuration).

docs.title: One implementation, every binding
docs.text: Telemetry lives in the C++ runtime, beneath the public API, not in any one front-end. So every binding inherits it for free: the Java binding is fully observable today with no telemetry-specific code, and anything else built on the C ABI would consume the same stream the same way. There is no per-language telemetry to write or keep in sync; there is one implementation, in the core.

docs.title: What it gives you
docs.text:
• Per-rank frames: cumulative task counters (started / sent / received), tasks currently running, scheduler pending count, pool idle time split into starved and imbalanced, scheduler running and waiting time, the bytes and time spent moving tasks, process CPU %, RSS, thread count, and a per-destination traffic list (edges_out) for visualizing how work flows between ranks.
  • Per-host frames, emitted by one sentinel rank per host: per-socket CPU and memory, total/available memory, and the job's own memory usage and limit (from its enforcing cgroup, so a shared node shows gempba's allocation rather than the whole machine).
  • Topology snapshot, captured once at startup: every host, the ranks it owns, each rank's scheduler role, per-socket physical/logical core counts, CPU names, and CPU-id lists, plus a run object with the run's setup, annotations and markers. Frames carry numeric ranks; the topology maps them back to host and hardware.
  • Live control: a connected client can retune the one telemetry interval, pause, resume, snapshot or mark the run, and from v5.0.0 stop it with its token, on the fly, so a dashboard can dial detail up while you watch and back down for long unattended runs.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph hostA [host]
        W0[rank 0 / coordinator / sentinel]
        W1[rank 1 / worker]
        W2[rank 2 / worker]
    end
    W0 -->|record_* hooks| H0[hub, rank 0]
    W1 -->|record_* hooks| H1[hub, rank 1]
    W2 -->|record_* hooks| H2[hub, rank 2]
    H0 -->|frames, on the telemetry interval| AGG[aggregator, rank 0]
    H1 -->|frames, on the telemetry interval| AGG
    H2 -->|frames, on the telemetry interval| AGG
    AGG -->|line-delimited JSON, loopback TCP :9000| DASH[dashboard / watch script]
    DASH -.->|control messages| AGG
  • The hub (gempba::telemetry::telemetry_hub): one per process. Ranks feed it through lock-free record_* hot-path hooks; it snapshots the counters into frames on the telemetry interval and pushes them over the transport.
  • Transports, chosen by how the run is set up: an in-process local transport when it has no scheduler, and an MPI transport on a private communicator (MPI_Comm_dup, so telemetry never collides with application traffic) when it has one, auto-installed inside gempba::mpi::create_scheduler on every rank.
  • The aggregator: rank 0 aggregates every rank's frames and runs a loopback-only TCP server (default 127.0.0.1:9000) that broadcasts the merged stream as line-delimited JSON to any number of connected clients. That socket is the dashboard channel.

docs.title: Configuring telemetry
docs.text: Telemetry is on by default and needs no setup to start streaming. This page covers what you may want to change or add: whether it runs at all, which port the dashboard channel binds, how often frames are emitted, and the context you attach to a run.

docs.title: Turning it off (and on)
docs.text:
The kill switch is a process-local, sticky flag. Set it before the first node_manager / scheduler is created, i.e. before the hub is installed.

C++Java 
#include <gempba/gempba.hpp>

gempba::telemetry::disable();      // no hub is installed; no pump thread, no socket
// ... create_load_balancer / create_node_manager, or gempba::mpi::create_scheduler ...

gempba::telemetry::enable();       // lift a prior disable
bool on = gempba::telemetry::is_enabled();

import io.gempba.GemPBA;

GemPBA.disableTelemetry();
// ... createLoadBalancer / createNodeManager ...

GemPBA.enableTelemetry();
boolean on = GemPBA.isTelemetryEnabled();

Set it symmetrically across all ranks

The flag is process-local. In an MPI run, disabling telemetry on only some ranks will deadlock the still-enabled ranks during transport setup (the MPI transport sets up collectively). Call disable() on every rank, or none. The recommended pattern is to disable on all ranks before any create_* entry point.

docs.title: The dashboard port
docs.text:
The aggregator (rank 0) binds a loopback-only TCP server for the dashboard channel, at 127.0.0.1:9000 by default. Change it before the hub is installed:

C++Java 
#include <gempba/gempba.hpp>

gempba::telemetry::configure_port(9100);   // must be called before the first node_manager / scheduler

GemPBA.configureTelemetryPort(9100);       // in both artifacts, gempba and gempba-mpi

The server binds loopback only by design; it is never exposed on a public interface. To reach it from another machine, use the GemPBA Dashboard, which opens the SSH forward for you (see Connecting).

Two runs on the same host need different ports.

The examples take a port

Every gempba-examples program takes -telemetry_port <n>, and its scripts/run* read the TELEMETRY_PORT environment variable. gempba-java-examples' synthetic_void takes -Dgempba.telemetry.port=<n>, and its multiprocessing/run scripts take -port <n>. The two repositories' cluster jobs serve on 9001 and 9000, so both can run on one node. These options belong to the examples, not to the library; in your own code, call configure_port directly.

docs.title: Emission cadence and live control
docs.text:
gempba uses one telemetry interval. Rank frames, per-host (node) frames and the aggregator's broadcast all refresh on it: 500 ms by default, clamped to 50–600000 ms. Change it in code, or live from a connected client, so a UI can throttle the stream without restarting the run.

A connected client writes control lines back on the same socket, one JSON object per line:

Control line Effect {"kind":"set_interval_ms","value":N} Set the interval to N ms, for rank frames, node frames and the broadcast alike. {"kind":"pause"} Stop every rank sending frames. Counters keep counting, and the aggregator keeps sending a short "paused":true line so the run does not look lost. {"kind":"resume"} Resume at the current interval. {"kind":"snapshot"} Make every rank send one frame at once, whatever the interval and even while paused; the aggregator then broadcasts one full line. {"kind":"mark","label":"..."} Record a timestamped marker on the run, labelled as you choose. {"kind":"stop","token":"..."} Stop the run, from gempba v5.0.0: every rank prunes the work it hasn't started, and the run ends with its best result so far. Accepted only when token matches the GEMPBA_STOP_TOKEN environment variable the run was started with; see Stopping a Run.

In code, the equivalent setter lives on the hub:

auto* hub = gempba::telemetry::get();      // nullptr if telemetry is disabled
if (hub) {
    hub->set_interval_ms(250);             // rank frames, node frames and the broadcast
}

The in-process control enum is control_kind::SET_INTERVAL_MS.

A faster interval gives a more responsive dashboard at the cost of more frames on the wire; a slower one is cheaper for long unattended runs. Because the interval is client-controllable, a dashboard can dial it up while you are watching and back down when you are not.

docs.title: Annotating and marking a run
docs.text:
Two C++ calls attach context to a run, so the dashboard and any consumer can describe it and line events up against a timeline. Both reach the stream's run object (see Data model).

gempba::telemetry::annotate_run("experiment", "bitset-v3");  // up to 8 key/value pairs
gempba::telemetry::mark_run("phase 2 started");              // a timestamped marker
  • annotate_run(key, value) records up to 8 key/value strings (keys 1–32 bytes, values up to 64), shown under run.annotations. Set them before or during the run; setting a key again overwrites it.
  • mark_run(label) records a timestamped marker under run.markers, tagged source "code" (labels 1–64 bytes, at most 32 per run). A connected client records one the same way with the {"kind":"mark","label":"..."} control line, tagged source "dashboard".

docs.title: Connecting to the stream
docs.text:
The aggregator (rank 0) broadcasts telemetry as line-delimited JSON over a loopback-only TCP socket (default 127.0.0.1:9000). Any number of clients can connect and each receives the same stream. This page shows how to tail a local run. To watch a run on another machine, use the GemPBA Dashboard, which opens the SSH forward for you, jump host and MFA included.

GemPBA ships one helper script in the gempba repo's scripts/ directory, in both PowerShell and bash: telemetry_view (live-tail). Use the .ps1 on Windows or the .sh on Linux/macOS.

docs.title: Local run
docs.text:
While a GemPBA program is running on your machine, tail its stream:

PowerShellBash 
scripts\telemetry_view.ps1             # connects to 127.0.0.1:9000
scripts\telemetry_view.ps1 -Port 9100  # if the run used a non-default port

scripts/telemetry_view.sh              # connects to 127.0.0.1:9000
scripts/telemetry_view.sh --port 9100  # if the run used a non-default port

telemetry_view prints one row per rank, each tagged with its role (coordinator or worker) and refreshed in place every interval: that rank's task counters, running tasks, thread count, CPU % and resident memory. While the run is paused it marks the paused stretch rather than blanking, and it prints each run marker as it arrives. The bash version shows times on macOS too. For the full payload (topology, the run setup and every per-rank field), pass -Raw / --raw to print pretty JSON instead.

Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost

The aggregator binds IPv4 loopback. On Windows, localhost may resolve to IPv6 (::1) first and fail to connect, so always target 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Remote run
docs.text: Reaching a run on another machine is the dashboard's job. The GemPBA Dashboard opens the SSH forward itself, including the jump-host hop and the MFA prompt, with no scripts to run and no port to forward by hand. See the dashboard's Connect section for the direct-host and jump-host setups.

docs.title: Custom clients
docs.text:
Nothing about the protocol is tied to the helper script; it is just newline-delimited JSON on a TCP socket. Any language that can open a socket and split on newlines can consume it, or you can tail it by hand:

nc 127.0.0.1 9000          # or: socat - TCP:127.0.0.1:9000
nc 127.0.0.1 9000 | jq .   # pretty-print each frame

To consume a remote run from your own client, forward the port over SSH first (ssh -L 9000:127.0.0.1:9000 user@host, adding -J user@login-node for a jump host), then connect locally.

The Data model covers the JSON shape at a glance, and gempba's docs/telemetry/wire-format.md is the full field reference a custom consumer parses.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
Let me tell you a storyWhen I was doing my master's, I was building GemPBA and testing it the only way that felt honest: by throwing real branch-and-bound problems at it on a real cluster. That sounds clean. It was not.

Most weeks went one of two ways. Either I was designing the next steps of an algorithm, or I was deep in the library hunting a bug, and the cruel part was that I could rarely tell which one I was actually doing. A run would come back wrong and I would sit there with two suspects and no alibi for either: was my library broken, or was the algorithm I was using to test the library broken? Some days it was one. Some days it was both. Most days I just did not know, and "I do not know" is the most expensive sentence in research.

So I would do what you do. I would write the batch script, set the resources, and submit it to SLURM. And then I would wait. Not minutes. Sometimes days, watching my job sit in the queue behind everyone else's, refreshing the status like it owed me money.

Finally my turn would come. The job would start. Hours would pass. I would go to sleep telling myself that this time the numbers would make sense.

They would not. The run would fail, or it would finish and quietly lie to me. And when I went digging, I would find the thing that still makes my stomach drop to remember: I had fat-fingered a setting, or misused my own library, and out of the hundreds of cores I had reserved, exactly one had done any work. One. A framework whose entire reason to exist is to use all of them, running like a single sad thread, while everything else I had been allocated sat there glowing and idle.

And here is the part nobody warns you about. Those idle cores were not free. They were mine, locked away from every other student and researcher who could have been using them while I was busy being wrong. The scheduler remembers that. Your fair share drops, and the next time you submit you wait even longer. I had paid for nothing, and then I paid for it again.

The worst of it was the blindness. Once a job is running on a cluster, it is a sealed box. You cannot see inside. You cannot tell whether the machine is roaring or asleep. You wait, and you hope, and you find out at the very end whether the last three days of your life meant anything.

So one day I tried to fix the blindness by hand. I spent an entire day, not on my research, on a script: something that would sit on the login node, find every compute node my job had been handed, reach into each one, open htop, and throw all of those terminals back onto my screen so I could watch them at once.

It was never a tool you could simply run. I had to be logged into the login node. It was all raw command line, spawning terminal after terminal, and then it was on me to drag them into place, tile them into a wall of little green bars, and sit there reading them like an air traffic controller, trying to judge from across the room whether every node was really working or whether half of them had quietly gone to sleep. It worked, in the way a thing held together with tape works: a full day of effort for a window I had to rebuild and rearrange for every single run, that demanded I keep staring at it, and that went dark the moment I looked away.

I got tired of finding out at the end. And I was done rebuilding that same fragile little window by hand every time I needed to look.

So I built the part I had always been missing: a way to watch the run while it happens.

The GemPBA Dashboard is a desktop app that connects to a running GemPBA program and shows the whole run live: every node and every rank, the cores working, the tasks started and moved each second, where the idle time goes, and the memory. It reads the same telemetry stream the runtime already broadcasts, so any GemPBA program is observable in it with no extra code.

Needs gempba v4.3.0 or later

Dashboard 2.0 reads telemetry schema 2, which gempba sends from v4.3.0 on, v5.0.0 included. For gempba v4.2.x and earlier, use dashboard 1.x. v5.0.0's additions, how a run ended and stopping it with its token, come with the dashboard's next release; 2.0 ignores them.

The Grid: the run summed up on top, one tile per node below, here connected through a jump host to four compute nodes.

v2.0.0 · MIT · built on Eclipse Theia and Electron, in the open: every release is compiled by GitHub Actions from the tagged source. Source: rapastranac/gempba-dashboard.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Grid sums the run up on top: the cores busy, the tasks started each second with their history, the tasks moved between ranks and across nodes, how idle the task-running ranks are, the memory, and how the run is set up (scheduler, load balancer, ranks, threads, gempba version). Below, one tile per node shows its CPU and history, its tasks started, its memory, and the tasks it sent and received. A node whose ranks stop sending fades on its own.
  • Cards lists the run as a node, socket and rank tree and shows the picked row as a live panel: a rank's CPU on the cores it may use, its tasks, its idle time and where it goes, its memory, its thread pool, its busiest peers, and its totals since the run started. The rank that coordinates the run, the aggregator and each node's sentinel are named as such.
  • Charts are yours to arrange, three to a row: CPU, memory, idle time, tasks (started, run locally, sent and received) and bytes, each as a rate or a running total. Add, swap, move or remove them, or drag one onto another. Every rank shares one layout and every node another, kept across restarts.
Cards: the node, socket and rank tree beside a selected rank's live panel and its charts. From a Grid tile into Cards, then arranging a rank's charts and checking its busiest peers.

Data that stops still makes sense. When a run pauses, ends, or the connection drops, the views keep what they last showed, fully usable and dimmed a little, under a bar that says why and since when: Paused, Run ended, Reconnecting…, or Not live with its cause. Nothing clears until you press Clear or listen again.

Stop listening and the views hold their last state, dimmed, under a bar that says why and since when. What the stream can be doing, and what each state keeps on screen.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
gempba serves its telemetry on a loopback port on whatever machine rank 0 runs on. The dashboard reaches that port one of three ways, chosen in the Connection view:

Local, Host, or Jump host: the same stream, reached three ways.
  • Local: gempba runs on this machine; just Listen on its port. No session needed.
  • Host: gempba runs on a VM or box you reach over SSH (user@host[:port]).
  • Jump host: gempba runs on a compute node behind a login node, as on an HPC cluster. The dashboard signs in to the login node, which reaches the compute node with the cluster's own SSH trust.

SSH uses your keys and known_hosts in ~/.ssh, asks to trust a new host once, and prompts for passphrases and MFA codes in a dialog. If the session drops, the dashboard says so and lets you connect again.

Jump-host mode nests the hop rather than using SSH ProxyJump, so it works even when only the login node is reachable and it enforces MFA:

Why jump-host mode nests the hop instead of using ProxyJump. Listening to a local run, then folding the Connection view away to give the run the whole window. Through a jump host: trust the login node once, answer the MFA prompt, and listen on the compute node.

The gempba port must match the one the run bound (see Configuration). Rank 0 names the host it serves on when it starts: telemetry listening on 127.0.0.1:9000 on host <name>.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
• Connection (the plug icon) holds four panels: Session (Local, Host or Jump host, and for SSH the host, port and key), Target (the compute node and gempba's port, then Listen), Refresh rate (a preset or your own, in milliseconds), and Run (Pause/Resume, Snapshot, a labelled Mark, and Clear data).
  • Grid: click a tile to select its node; double-click, or press Enter, to open it in Cards. Cards: pick a row for its panel, and shape the layout from the Charts button and each chart's menu.
  • The status bar sums the stream up, such as 4 nodes · 26.6k tasks/s · 500 ms, and clicking it exposes the live controls. Every command is also in the palette (F1) as GemPBA: …, and Settings (the gear) lists GemPBA's options, including the built-in GemPBA Light and Dark themes.

Change the cadence without touching the run. One refresh rate drives every frame, and the dashboard pushes it to the running job over the open connection. gempba is compiled into your application, so a job already on a cluster is a fixed binary, yet you can dial detail up while you watch and back down when you step away, with no recompile, restart, or resubmit. This is the client side of the runtime's live cadence control.

Changing the refresh rate, pausing, taking a snapshot and marking a moment, then stopping from the status bar. Previewing the built-in themes live, then switching to GemPBA Dark and back to GemPBA Light.

docs.title: The data path
docs.text:
Each feature is an Eclipse Theia extension plugged into one telemetry hub. A rank's frames reach rank 0, which sends one line per interval; the dashboard maps each line to a snapshot for the window, where the hub keeps the histories the views draw, and the controls travel back the same way.

From a rank's frame to the chart on screen, and controls back the other way.

The repo's ARCHITECTURE.md walks through the packages and the extension model, and DeepWiki is an AI-assisted tour of the source.

docs.title: Headless or scripted?
docs.text: If you want the stream without a GUI (a terminal tail, a log, a custom consumer), the bundled telemetry_view script and the raw JSON protocol are documented under Connecting and Data model.

docs.title: Source and license
docs.text: rapastranac/gempba-dashboard, MIT, built on Eclipse Theia and Electron. Issues and contributions are welcome there. Every published installer is built by GitHub Actions from the tagged source.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Telemetry is exposed two ways, and both carry the same information:

  • In process, as C++ frame structs (<gempba/telemetry/frames.hpp>, topology.hpp) for a consumer compiled into the same binary, which reads them from the process's hub (gempba::telemetry::get()).
  • Over the socket, as a line-delimited JSON broadcast on the dashboard channel, for everything else.

This page is a map of what a broadcast line carries. The authoritative, field-by-field reference, with each key's unit and the release that added it, every control line, the compatibility rules and every schema version, lives in gempba's docs/telemetry/wire-format.md. This page links there rather than keeping a second copy in sync.

docs.title: Schema 2
docs.text: gempba sends schema 2 from v4.3.0 on, v5.0.0 included: every line carries "version": 2. A consumer written against an older release reads that release's schema, which stays valid for it. wire-format.md lists every schema version, newest first, and the compatibility rules: a consumer ignores keys it does not know, and a renamed, removed or redefined key bumps version.

docs.title: What a line carries
docs.text:
The aggregator (rank 0) emits one JSON object per line, every telemetry interval. A full line is self-contained, so a client that connects late misses nothing but history:

  • an envelope: version, run_id, ts, elapsed_seconds, paused and final, and on the final line end;
  • the topology: each host, each rank's identity with its role (coordinator or worker), and a run object holding the run's setup, its annotations and its markers;
  • ranks: the latest frame from every rank, whatever its role: task counters, where its pool threads' idle time went (starved versus imbalanced), scheduler timing, the cost of moving tasks, and an edges_out list of the ranks it sent tasks to;
  • nodes: the latest per-host frame from each host's sentinel rank: CPU, memory, and the job's own memory within its cgroup.

While the run is paused, a line carries only the envelope header with "paused": true. The line sent at shutdown carries the run's totals and "final": true, and is the last before the aggregator closes the connection. From gempba v5.0.0, the final line also says how the run ended in end: reason, and for an interrupted run trigger and signal. A connection that closes without that final line was lost; see Stopping a Run. See the full worked example and every field.

docs.title: Controlling the stream
docs.text: The socket is bidirectional: a client writes control lines back, one JSON object per line, to set the telemetry interval, to pause, resume, snapshot or mark the run, or, from gempba v5.0.0, to stop it. Configuration covers them from the runtime side; wire-format.md gives the exact lines a client sends.

docs.title: JSON keys versus C++ struct fields
docs.text: The JSON keys and the C++ struct fields describe the same data, and since v5.0.0 they use the same words: the line's rank is rank_frame's m_rank, and its idle_microseconds_per_thread is m_idle_microseconds_per_thread. They still don't always share a name. Read the wire names from wire-format.md and the struct names from the gempba headers; do not derive one from the other by stripping an m_ prefix.

docs.title: Feeding telemetry from your own scheduler
docs.text: A custom scheduler reaches this same stream through gempba's record_*() calls. gempba's docs/telemetry/custom-schedulers.md says what a custom scheduler must do for its runs to show up, and which call fills which key.
